docs.title: Mobile Testing Basics
docs.text: Testing mobile applications requires validating unique parameters like screen orientation, network switching, battery health, and platform-specific UI interactions.

docs.title: 1. Native Mobile Apps
docs.text: Built specifically for a single mobile OS using platform languages (Swift/Objective-C for iOS, Kotlin/Java for Android). - Pros: Maximum performance, full access to device hardware (GPS, camera, sensors). - Cons: High development cost (two separate codebases).

docs.title: 2. Mobile Web Apps
docs.text: Websites optimized for mobile browsers. They do not reside on the device; users access them via URL. - Pros: Instant deployments, single codebase. - Cons: Zero hardware access, completely dependent on network stability.

docs.title: 3. Hybrid Mobile Apps
docs.text: A wrapper container (like Cordova, Capacitor, or Ionic) hosting a standard web application inside a native shell. - Pros: Code once, run on both platform stores. - Cons: Lower performance, complicated hardware integrations.

docs.title: Core Mobile Specific Testing Parameters
docs.text:
• Interruption Testing: How does the app handle sudden alerts? (Incoming calls, text alerts, low battery warnings, chargers being connected).
  • Screen Rotations: Smooth transitions between Portrait and Landscape views without crashing or data loss.
  • Network Profiling: Transitioning from Wi-Fi to 4G/5G, and losing connection entirely (offline mode check).
  • Store Guidelines: Adherence to Apple App Store or Google Play Store deployment policies.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Always verify the offline mode behaviors of mobile apps.
  • Native applications require extensive regression tests since users must manually update store versions.
  • Test app behavior during low memory/battery conditions.
  • Related: Appium Setup Guide.

docs.title: What is Appium?
docs.text:
Appium is an open-source, cross-platform test automation tool used to validate Native, Hybrid, and Mobile Web applications on iOS and Android.

"Appium lets you write tests against mobile platforms using the standard W3C WebDriver API—the same philosophy behind Selenium."

docs.title: Key Architectural Pipeline
docs.text: [ Appium Script (Java/Python) ] ──→ [ Appium Server ] ──→ [ UI Automator (Android) / XCUITest (iOS) ] ──→ [ Device ]

docs.title: Step 1: Install Appium Server
docs.text: npm install -g appium

docs.title: Step 2: Install Appium Python Client
docs.text: pip install Appium-Python-Client

docs.title: Step 3: Configure Android Home Paths
docs.text:
Ensure your environment variables are configured in .bashrc or .zshrc: 

export ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/Android/Sdk
export PATH=$PATH:$ANDROID_HOME/emulator
export PATH=$PATH:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools

docs.title: Step 4: Write Your First Appium Script
docs.text:
Create a file named test_appium_android.py:

# test_appium_android.py
from appium import webdriver
from appium.options.android import UiAutomator2Options

def test_android_calc():
    # 1. Define target capabilities
    options = UiAutomator2Options()
    options.platform_name = "Android"
    options.device_name = "emulator-5554"
    options.app_package = "com.android.calculator2"
    options.app_activity = ".Calculator"

    # 2. Initialize driver session pointing to local Appium server
    driver = webdriver.Remote("http://localhost:4723", options=options)

    try:
        # 3. Perform clicks (Standard Selenium syntax!)
        driver.find_element(by="id", value="com.android.calculator2:id/digit_7").click()
        print("Successfully interacted with emulator!")

    finally:
        driver.quit()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_android_calc()

docs.title: Appium Inspector
docs.text: A vital desktop companion GUI tool used to inspect elements, discover UI resource-ids, and record actions directly on the active mobile screen.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Appium utilizes W3C WebDriver selectors—making the syntax identical to Selenium.
  • Always use UiAutomator2Options for Android and XCUITestOptions for iOS.
  • Appium Inspector is crucial for identifying target locators.

docs.title: Emulator vs. Simulator vs. Real Device
docs.text: Selecting the right device platform to run mobile tests is key to keeping execution costs balanced while maintaining QA accuracy.

docs.title: Core Definitions
docs.text:
• Simulator: A software program that mimics the behavioral characteristics of an OS. It does not replicate the exact device hardware (common in Apple Xcode simulators).
  • Emulator: A software program that emulates both the OS and the exact device hardware at the binary level (common in Android Studio Virtual Devices).
  • Real Device: The actual hardware phone (e.g., iPhone 15, Samsung S24) in a tester's hand or hosted on a device cloud grid.

docs.title: The Selection Matrix
docs.text: Parameter Simulator Emulator Real Device Speed ⚡ Extremely Fast Slower (Heavy CPU load) Fast Cost 🟢 Free / Low 🟢 Free / Low 🔴 Extremely Expensive Hardware Accuracy 🔴 Low (Uses host CPU/RAM) 🟡 Medium 🟢 100% Perfect Best Used For Fast UI/UX verification Basic functional regressions Final sanity, performance, security

docs.title: Strategic QA Recommendation
docs.text:
Phase 1: Feature development & fast sanity
  ──→ Use SIMULATORS / EMULATORS (Fast, cost-efficient)

Phase 2: Complete integration & nightly pipelines
  ──→ Use Cloud Device Grids (e.g., BrowserStack, SauceLabs)

Phase 3: Final Pre-Release Check
  ──→ Run tests on REAL DEVICES (Validate battery, CPU heat, interruptions)

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Simulators are fast but lack hardware integrity.
  • Emulators are excellent for functional verification but consume massive computer CPU/RAM.
  • Real Devices are mandatory for final sanity, hardware integrations (e.g., Bluetooth, Camera), and performance profile validation.

docs.title: 🗄️ Database Testing
docs.text: This section covers database and back-end testing fundamentals, ACID compliance validation, schema verification, data mapping, and common validation queries.

docs.title: 🗂️ Files in this Section
docs.text:
• 01_db_testing_fundamentals.md — What is Database Testing? (UI vs. DB layer)
  • 02_data_integrity_validation.md — Primary/Foreign keys, null checks, constraints
  • 03_acid_properties_validation.md — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability checks
  • 04_migration_and_schema_testing.md — Verifying schema updates and rollbacks

docs.title: What is Database Testing?
docs.text: Database Testing is a back-end testing type that validates the schema, tables, triggers, indexes, stored procedures, and data integrity of the database. It ensures that the application layer records data accurately without corruption.

docs.title: Front-End (UI) vs. Back-End (DB) Testing
docs.text: Parameter UI Testing Database Testing Interface Direct graphical interface (browser, mobile screen) Query interfaces (SQL prompt, backend drivers) Focus Buttons, form fills, styling layout, workflow Schema constraints, table structures, ACID compliance Speed Slower (requires rendering) ⚡ Extremely Fast Key Threat Caught UI validation misses, broken buttons Duplicate primary keys, orphaned foreign keys

docs.title: 1. Structural Layer
docs.text: Validating the structural elements of the database: - Schema updates, Table relationships (1:many, many:many). - Primary and Foreign key constraints. - Trigger behavior (automatic update scripts).

docs.title: 2. Functional Layer
docs.text: Verifying the data transactions: - CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) are saved accurately. - Transactions rollback if an intermediate step fails. - Stored Procedures evaluate mathematically correct logic.

docs.title: 3. Non-Functional Layer
docs.text:
• Load Testing: Running complex SQL query checks under heavy database read/write volume.
  • Security: Verifying user access permissions and database privilege levels.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• UI testing is never enough—always verify backend databases to ensure data mapping is correct.
  • Stored procedures should have isolated unit checks.
  • Keep test data generation isolated from real databases.

docs.title: Data Integrity Validation
docs.text: Data Integrity is the assurance that digital data remains accurate, consistent, and reliable over its entire lifecycle.

docs.title: 1. Entity Integrity (Primary Keys)
docs.text: Ensures that each table has a Primary Key that is unique and not null. - QA Check: Attempt to insert two records with identical IDs. The database must reject the second transaction with a Unique Constraint Violation.

docs.title: 2. Referential Integrity (Foreign Keys)
docs.text: Ensures that relationships between tables remain consistent. A foreign key in Table B must point to a valid primary key in Table A. - QA Check: Attempt to insert an order record for a user ID that does not exist. The database must block the write with a Foreign Key Constraint Violation. - Delete Check: Attempt to delete a user record who has active orders. Check if the database blocks the deletion or cascades the delete successfully based on the business strategy.

docs.title: 3. Domain Integrity (Data Types)
docs.text: Ensures that columns accept values only within a defined structure or set. - QA Check: Attempt to save alphabetic text inside a price (decimal) or age (integer) column.

docs.title: 4. User-Defined Integrity (Business Rules)
docs.text: Custom constraints set by developer specifications. - Example: Ensuring the discount column is never greater than the price column. - QA Check: Run boundary testing on custom database constraints.

docs.title: Standard Integrity Verification Queries
docs.text:
-- Check for orphaned orders (broken referential integrity)
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM users);
-- Expected result: 0 rows returned

-- Check for null constraints on required fields
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE email IS NULL OR created_at IS NULL;
-- Expected result: 0 rows returned

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Database constraint checks prevent dirty data from corrupting reports.
  • Validate Cascading Deletes carefully to avoid orphaned records.
  • Input validation on front-end controls helps, but backend database constraints are the ultimate gatekeeper.

docs.title: ACID Properties Validation
docs.text: Any relational database (RDBMS) processing transactions must adhere to ACID properties to guarantee absolute data reliability.

docs.title: The ACID Definition
docs.text:
A ──→ Atomicity (All or nothing)
    C ──→ Consistency (Valid state transition)
    I ──→ Isolation (Concurrent transactions don't interfere)
    D ──→ Durability (Once saved, it is safe from crashes)

docs.title: 1. Atomicity (All or Nothing)
docs.text: A transaction is considered a single, indivisible unit. If one step of a transaction fails, the entire transaction is cancelled, and the database rolls back to its initial state. - Example: transferring ₹1,000 from Account A to Account B. - Step 1: Deduct ₹1,000 from A. (Succeeds) - Step 2: Add ₹1,000 to B. (Fails due to network drop) - QA Check: Force a failure during Step 2. Verify that Account A’s balance rolls back (₹1,000 is restored).

docs.title: 2. Consistency
docs.text: A transaction must move the database from one valid state to another, preserving all schema rules and constraints. - QA Check: Verify that invalid transactions (e.g., trying to set balance to negative when constraint is balance >= 0) are rejected, keeping the database consistent.

docs.title: 3. Isolation
docs.text: Concurrently executed transactions should not interfere with one another. The execution state should look as if they ran sequentially. - QA Check: Simulating race conditions. If two users click to purchase the last remaining stock at the exact same millisecond, verify that only one transaction succeeds, and the second transaction receives a "Sold Out" validation block.

docs.title: 4. Durability
docs.text: Once a transaction is committed, it remains saved in database logs even if the server crashes immediately afterward. - QA Check: Force a hard shutdown or server restart immediately after a massive batch transaction is committed. Upon reboot, verify that all committed records are present in the tables.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Atomicity is tested by injecting failures mid-transaction.
  • Isolation is tested using concurrent load generators to check for race conditions.
  • Relational databases (PostgreSQL, Oracle) offer strict ACID compliance out of the box, but business code configurations (e.g., transactional annotations) can still break them.

docs.title: 🚀 CI/CD & DevOps Integration
docs.text: This section covers Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, automated execution setups, and pipeline scripting using GitHub Actions and Jenkins.

docs.title: 🗂️ Files in this Section
docs.text:
• 01_ci_cd_fundamentals.md — Why automate execution? (Shift-Left validation)
  • 02_github_actions_workflow.md — Complete .github/workflows/ YAML guides
  • 03_jenkins_pipeline_setup.md — Declarative Jenkinsfile pipeline patterns
  • 04_containerized_testing_docker.md — Containerizing test environments with Docker

docs.title: CI/CD Integration Fundamentals
docs.text: Automated test cases are only valuable if they run automatically. Integrating testing inside CI/CD pipelines ensures that every code change is validated before reaching users.

docs.title: The DevOps Loop: Continuous Quality
docs.text:
Code Check-in (Git) ──→ Build Triggered ──→ Automated Testing ──→ Deploy to Production
                                               (Quality Gate)
  1. Continuous Integration (CI): Developers merge code changes to main multiple times a day. The CI server compiles the code, executes unit tests, and packages build artifacts.
  2. Quality Gate (QA): The pipeline deploys the build artifact to a QA environment and runs automated Smoke & Integration test suites. If tests fail, the pipeline immediately halts, blockading the bad code.
  3. Continuous Deployment (CD): Once all tests pass green, the pipeline deploys the artifact straight to staging or production.

docs.title: Benefits of Pipeline Integration
docs.text:
• Immediate Feedback: Developers know they broke a feature within 5 minutes of merging code.
  • Eliminate "Works on my machine": Automated scripts run in standardized virtual containers (e.g., Docker).
  • Safe Releases: No manual steps mean human deployment mistakes are eliminated.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Test automation must sit inside the CI pipeline to be valuable.
  • Fail early—run fast unit tests first, and deferred heavier UI regressions later.
  • If a test is flaky, it should be disabled or quarantined to avoid pipeline fatigue.

docs.title: What is GitHub Actions?
docs.text: GitHub Actions is a native CI/CD orchestration engine built directly inside GitHub. It allows you to build, test, and deploy code directly from repository event triggers (e.g., Pull Requests, Push).

docs.title: Complete Pytest Workflow Config
docs.text:
Create a file named .github/workflows/pytest_runner.yml:

# .github/workflows/pytest_runner.yml
name: QA Test Execution Suite

# 1. Define events that trigger the pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, develop ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]
  workflow_dispatch: # Allows manual trigger from GitHub UI

# 2. Define execution jobs
jobs:
  run-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    # Step 1: Clone repository code
    - name: Checkout Code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    # Step 2: Configure Python
    - name: Set up Python
      uses: actions/setup-python@v5
      with:
        python-version: '3.10'

    # Step 3: Cache Pip Dependencies to speed up runs
    - name: Cache Pip Dependencies
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.cache/pip
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('**/requirements.txt') }}

    # Step 4: Install Dependencies
    - name: Install Dependencies
      run: |
        python -m pip install --upgrade pip
        pip install -r requirements.txt

    # Step 5: Run Tests using Pytest
    - name: Execute Pytest Suite
      run: |
        pytest -m smoke --html=reports/smoke_report.html --self-contained-html

    # Step 6: Publish HTML Report as Build Artifact
    - name: Upload Test Report
      if: always() # Always run this step even if tests fail!
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: execution-report
        path: reports/smoke_report.html

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Use actions/cache to speed up build durations.
  • Set if: always() on report upload steps to ensure test logs are preserved even when test assertions fail.
  • Secrets (like API keys or passwords) must be stored in GitHub Repository Secrets and injected as environment variables.

docs.title: What is Jenkins?
docs.text: Jenkins is the most popular self-hosted open-source automation server used to configure custom CI/CD pipelines.

docs.title: Declarative Jenkinsfile Pipeline Pattern
docs.text:
Create a file named Jenkinsfile in the root of your project repository:

// Jenkinsfile (Declarative Syntax)
pipeline {
    agent {
        // Run execution steps in a standardized Docker container
        docker { 
            image 'python:3.10-slim' 
        }
    }

    environment {
        BASE_URL = 'https://qa.ecommerce-demo.com'
        // Bind secrets securely from Jenkins Credentials Store
        DB_PASSWORD = credentials('qa-db-password')
    }

    stages {
        stage('Checkout') {
            steps {
                // Pull code from git
                checkout scm
            }
        }

        stage('Install Dependencies') {
            steps {
                sh 'pip install -r requirements.txt'
            }
        }

        stage('Execute Tests') {
            steps {
                // Execute pytest regression marker
                sh 'pytest -m regression --junitxml=results.xml'
            }
        }
    }

    post {
        always {
            // Archive and display test results inside Jenkins UI
            junit 'results.xml'
        }
        success {
            echo "SUCCESS: All regression test cases passed successfully!"
        }
        failure {
            echo "FAILURE: Tests failed! Alerting Slack channels..."
            // Code block to send Slack notification
        }
    }
}

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Jenkins Declarative pipelines are configured via a Jenkinsfile saved in source control.
  • Use Docker agents to guarantee identical runtime environments.
  • Use the post block to automatically publish test reports (junit format) and trigger slack alerts on failures.

docs.title: 🛠️ Testing Tools
docs.text: This section provides an overview of the most popular tools used in the software testing industry, categorized by their primary function.

docs.title: 🗂️ Files in this Section
docs.text:
• 01_test_management_tools.md — TestRail, Zephyr, Xray
  • 02_defect_tracking_tools.md — Jira, Bugzilla, Azure DevOps
  • 03_test_automation_tools.md — Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, Appium
  • 04_performance_testing_tools.md — JMeter, k6, LoadRunner
  • 05_api_testing_tools.md — Postman, REST Assured, SoapUI

docs.title: Test Management Tools
docs.text: Test Management tools help QA teams organize, track, and execute test cases, as well as manage test cycles and report on testing progress.

docs.title: 1. TestRail
docs.text:
• Overview: A comprehensive web-based test case management tool.
  • Key Features: Easy test case creation, execution tracking, powerful reporting, and seamless integration with Jira.
  • Best For: Teams looking for a dedicated, standalone test management platform with deep metrics.

docs.title: 2. Zephyr (Scale & Squad)
docs.text:
• Overview: A test management solution that lives directly inside Jira.
  • Key Features: Native Jira look and feel, linking test cases directly to user stories and bugs, real-time metrics on Jira dashboards.
  • Best For: Agile teams heavily invested in the Jira ecosystem.

docs.title: 3. Xray
docs.text:
• Overview: Another powerful test management app built directly into Jira, highly popular for BDD.
  • Key Features: Native support for Cucumber/Gherkin tests, full requirements traceability, and excellent REST API for CI/CD integration.
  • Best For: Teams practicing BDD and looking for advanced Jira integration.

docs.title: 4. Azure Test Plans
docs.text:
• Overview: The test management module within Azure DevOps.
  • Key Features: Rich manual exploratory testing tools, traceability matrix, and tight integration with Azure Repos and Pipelines.
  • Best For: Teams fully utilizing the Microsoft Azure DevOps ecosystem.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The choice of a test management tool often depends heavily on the company's existing project management software (e.g., Jira, Azure DevOps).
  • A good test management tool must support Requirements Traceability to link tests to user stories.

docs.title: Defect Tracking Tools
docs.text: Defect tracking tools are essential for logging, prioritizing, and managing the lifecycle of software bugs from discovery to resolution.

docs.title: 1. Jira Software
docs.text:
• Overview: The industry standard for Agile project management and bug tracking.
  • Key Features: Highly customizable workflows, Scrum/Kanban boards, extensive marketplace integrations.
  • Best For: Almost any modern software development team.

docs.title: 2. Bugzilla
docs.text:
• Overview: A classic, open-source bug tracking system developed by Mozilla.
  • Key Features: Extremely stable, lightweight, email notifications, and completely free.
  • Best For: Open-source projects or teams needing a free, robust, no-frills tracker.

docs.title: 3. Azure Boards (Azure DevOps)
docs.text:
• Overview: Microsoft's Agile planning and defect tracking tool.
  • Key Features: Kanban boards, backlogs, team dashboards, and seamless integration with Git and Azure Pipelines.
  • Best For: Microsoft-centric development shops.

docs.title: 4. GitHub Issues / GitLab Issues
docs.text:
• Overview: Built-in issue trackers living alongside the source code repository.
  • Key Features: Lightweight, developers can close issues directly via commit messages (e.g., Fixes #102), label management.
  • Best For: Open-source projects, smaller teams, or developer-heavy workflows where simplicity is preferred over complex workflows.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Regardless of the tool, a defect must move through a structured lifecycle (New $\to$ In Progress $\to$ In QA $\to$ Closed).
  • Jira is the undisputed king of enterprise defect tracking; mastering its JQL (Jira Query Language) is a highly valued QA skill.

docs.title: Test Automation Tools
docs.text: Automation tools are used to execute pre-scripted tests on software applications, reducing manual effort and increasing regression speed.

docs.title: 1. Selenium WebDriver
docs.text:
• Overview: The grandfather of web automation. Open-source API that interacts directly with browser drivers.
  • Languages: Java, Python, C#, JavaScript, Ruby.
  • Best For: Cross-browser testing, legacy applications, teams wanting ultimate control over framework architecture.

docs.title: 2. Playwright
docs.text:
• Overview: Modern, open-source tool by Microsoft using the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP).
  • Languages: JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Java, C#.
  • Best For: Modern web apps (React, Angular), teams needing lightning-fast execution and auto-waiting.

docs.title: 3. Cypress
docs.text:
• Overview: Developer-centric tool that runs tests directly inside the browser.
  • Languages: JavaScript/TypeScript.
  • Best For: Front-end developers, teams needing "time-travel" debugging and highly visual test runners.

docs.title: 1. Appium
docs.text:
• Overview: The leading open-source tool for automating native, mobile web, and hybrid applications on iOS mobile, Android mobile, and Windows desktop platforms.
  • Architecture: Uses the WebDriver protocol, allowing you to use standard Selenium commands for mobile apps.
  • Best For: Cross-platform mobile testing using a single codebase.

docs.title: 2. Espresso (Android) & XCUITest (iOS)
docs.text:
• Overview: Native testing frameworks built into Android Studio and Xcode respectively.
  • Languages: Java/Kotlin (Espresso), Swift/Objective-C (XCUITest).
  • Best For: Developers doing deep, native platform testing where execution speed and deep hardware hooks are prioritized over cross-platform code sharing.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Selenium is the industry baseline, but Playwright is rapidly becoming the modern standard for web UI.
  • Appium rules the cross-platform mobile automation space.
  • The choice of tool should align with the programming language the development team uses to facilitate code reviews and collaboration.

docs.title: Performance Testing Tools
docs.text: Performance tools generate virtual users to simulate heavy load on applications, databases, and APIs to identify breaking points and latency bottlenecks.

docs.title: 1. Apache JMeter
docs.text:
• Overview: Open-source, Java-based desktop application designed for load testing functional behavior and measuring performance.
  • Key Features: Protocol support (HTTP, JDBC, FTP, SOAP), visual test plan creation, extensive plugins.
  • Best For: QA Engineers looking for a free, industry-standard tool with a graphical interface.

docs.title: 2. k6 (Grafana Labs)
docs.text:
• Overview: Modern, developer-centric, open-source load testing tool written in Go, using JavaScript for test scripting.
  • Key Features: "Code-first" approach, extremely low resource consumption, integrates perfectly into CI/CD pipelines, thresholds for pass/fail.
  • Best For: Developers and modern SDETs who prefer writing performance tests as code.

docs.title: 3. LoadRunner (Micro Focus)
docs.text:
• Overview: Enterprise-grade performance testing tool.
  • Key Features: Supports an massive array of legacy and modern protocols, highly accurate emulation, robust reporting.
  • Best For: Large enterprises, banks, and institutions willing to pay premium licensing for extensive protocol support and dedicated support.

docs.title: 4. Gatling
docs.text:
• Overview: Open-source load testing tool based on Scala, Akka, and Netty.
  • Key Features: High performance architecture, colorful HTML reports, scriptable in Scala or Java.
  • Best For: Teams embedded in the JVM/Scala ecosystem needing high-throughput load generation.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• JMeter is best for traditional QA teams needing a GUI.
  • k6 is the rising star for modern, "Performance as Code" integrated into DevOps pipelines.
  • Never run performance tests in GUI mode; always use CLI execution to save RAM.

docs.title: API Testing Tools
docs.text: API testing tools allow QA engineers to bypass the UI and validate business logic, security, and data handling directly at the integration layer.

docs.title: 1. Postman
docs.text:
• Overview: The undisputed king of manual API exploration and lightweight automation.
  • Key Features: Clean UI, environment variables, pre-request scripts, JavaScript assertions, collection runners (Newman).
  • Best For: Manual API testing, quick debugging, sharing API documentation, and basic CI/CD execution.

docs.title: 2. REST Assured
docs.text:
• Overview: A Java DSL (Domain Specific Language) for simplifying the testing of RESTful APIs.
  • Key Features: BDD syntax (Given/When/Then), powerful JSON/XML parsing, seamless integration with TestNG/JUnit.
  • Best For: Java-based automation teams looking to build robust, scalable API automation frameworks.

docs.title: 3. SoapUI (ReadyAPI)
docs.text:
• Overview: An advanced tool specifically designed for testing complex SOAP and REST web services.
  • Key Features: Automated WSDL parsing, data-driven testing, complex security/encryption testing, Groovy scripting.
  • Best For: Enterprises dealing heavily in legacy SOAP/XML services or complex financial APIs.

docs.title: 4. Pytest + Requests (Python)
docs.text:
• Overview: Using Python's standard requests library combined with the pytest testing framework.
  • Key Features: Ultimate flexibility, pure Python code, easy integration with database validation libraries (SQLAlchemy).
  • Best For: SDETs and QA Automation Engineers working in Python-centric environments.

docs.title: 📌 Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Every QA should have Postman installed for daily API exploration.
  • For enterprise automation, REST Assured (Java) or Pytest+Requests (Python) are the industry standards for building maintainable codebases.

docs.title: 🌍 Real-World Testing Projects
docs.text: This section provides complete, end-to-end testing artifacts for three distinct industry domains. These projects demonstrate how theory translates into professional practice.

docs.title: 🛒 Project 1: E-Commerce Platform
docs.text: A B2C retail web application. - Focus: Functional testing, UI automation, cart calculations, and payment gateway integration.

docs.title: 🏦 Project 2: Core Banking Application
docs.text: A highly secure financial ledger system. - Focus: Security testing, database data integrity, transaction ACID compliance, and role-based access control (RBAC).

docs.title: 🏥 Project 3: Healthcare API Portal
docs.text:
A backend integration portal for medical records (HL7/FHIR compliant). - Focus: API automation, data privacy (HIPAA compliance), and JSON schema validation.

Use these projects as a portfolio to demonstrate your practical QA skills during job interviews.

docs.title: E-Commerce Project: Bug Reports
docs.text: These are examples of professional bug reports logged during the System Testing phase of the E-Commerce project.

docs.title: BUG-101: Cart subtotal is calculated incorrectly when promo code is applied
docs.text:
• Status: Open
  • Severity: Major (S2)
  • Priority: High (P1)
  • Module: Cart / Checkout
  • Environment: Staging (v1.4.2)
  • Browser: Chrome v124 (Windows 11)

docs.title: Steps to Reproduce
docs.text:
1. Log in to the application.
  2. Add "Samsung Galaxy S24" ($1000) to the cart.
  3. Add "Phone Case" ($50) to the cart.
  4. Total is displayed as $1050.
  5. Apply promo code WELCOME10 (Designed for 10% off total order).

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
• The 10% discount ($105) should be applied to the total ($1050).
  • Final Total should be $945.

docs.title: Actual Result
docs.text:
• The 10% discount is only being applied to the first item in the cart ($100 off the phone).
  • The case remains full price.
  • Final Total is displayed as $950.

docs.title: Banking Application: Data Integrity Validation Queries
docs.text: In a banking context, backend database testing is as important as UI testing. Below are automated SQL queries used to validate the integrity of the ledger.

docs.title: 1. Verify Atomicity (Double-Entry Accounting)
docs.text:
In double-entry accounting, every debit must have a corresponding credit. The total sum of all transactions in the ledger must always equal zero.

-- QA Validation Query: Verify the ledger is balanced.
-- Expected Result: 0.00
SELECT SUM(amount) AS net_balance
FROM ledger_transactions;

docs.title: 2. Verify Account Balance Integrity
docs.text:
The cached "current balance" on the accounts table must exactly match the sum of all historical transactions for that account in the ledger.

-- QA Validation Query: Find accounts where the cached balance does NOT match the transaction history.
-- Expected Result: 0 rows returned
SELECT a.account_id, a.current_balance, SUM(t.amount) AS calculated_balance
FROM accounts a
JOIN ledger_transactions t ON a.account_id = t.account_id
GROUP BY a.account_id, a.current_balance
HAVING a.current_balance != SUM(t.amount);

docs.title: 3. Verify Negative Balance Constraints
docs.text:
Retail checking accounts should not be allowed to drop below $0.00 unless an overdraft protection flag is explicitly enabled.

-- QA Validation Query: Find retail accounts with negative balances that do not have overdraft enabled.
-- Expected Result: 0 rows returned
SELECT account_id, current_balance
FROM accounts
WHERE account_type = 'Retail_Checking' 
  AND current_balance < 0 
  AND overdraft_enabled = FALSE;

docs.title: 4. Verify Orphaned Transactions (Referential Integrity)
docs.text:
A transaction cannot exist if the parent account has been deleted. (The application should soft-delete accounts, not hard-delete).

-- QA Validation Query: Find transactions pointing to non-existent accounts.
-- Expected Result: 0 rows returned
SELECT transaction_id, account_id
FROM ledger_transactions
WHERE account_id NOT IN (SELECT account_id FROM accounts);

docs.title: Banking Application: Security Test Cases
docs.text: Below are critical security and boundary test cases specific to a banking environment.

docs.title: TC_SEC_01: Verify Session Timeout
docs.text:
• Priority: Critical
  • Steps:
  • Log in to the banking portal.
  • Leave the browser idle for exactly 15 minutes.
  • Attempt to click on "Transfer Funds".
  • Expected:
  • System intercepts the click.
  • User is immediately logged out.
  • Redirected to login page with message: "Session expired due to inactivity."

docs.title: TC_SEC_02: Verify Concurrent Login Handling
docs.text:
• Priority: High
  • Steps:
  • Log in to the application on Browser A (Chrome).
  • While keeping Browser A open, open Browser B (Firefox) on a different machine.
  • Attempt to log in with the exact same credentials.
  • Expected:
  • Login on Browser B is successful.
  • The active session on Browser A is immediately terminated.
  • If the user clicks anything on Browser A, they receive a "Session invalidated" error.

docs.title: TC_SEC_03: Verify SQL Injection on Fund Transfer Note Field
docs.text:
• Priority: Critical
  • Steps:
  • Log in and initiate a fund transfer.
  • In the "Optional Transfer Note" field, input: '; DROP TABLE transactions; --
  • Submit the transfer.
  • Expected:
  • Transfer is processed successfully.
  • The text is sanitized and stored literally as a string.
  • No database errors are thrown, and no tables are dropped.

docs.title: TC_SEC_04: Verify Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) Escalation
docs.text:
• Priority: Critical
  • Pre-conditions: Logged in as a standard retail customer.
  • Steps:
  • Identify the URL pattern for an admin dashboard (e.g., https://bank.com/user/dashboard).
  • Manually modify the URL in the browser address bar to https://bank.com/admin/dashboard.
  • Press Enter.
  • Expected:
  • User is blocked.
  • System returns a 403 Forbidden error.
  • Security event is logged in the backend audit trail.

docs.title: TC_SEC_05: Verify Race Condition on Withdrawals
docs.text:
• Priority: Critical
  • Pre-conditions: Account balance is exactly $100.
  • Steps:
  • Open the application on two different devices simultaneously.
  • Attempt to withdraw $100 on both devices at the exact same millisecond (using an automated script like JMeter to synchronize requests).
  • Expected:
  • Transaction isolation locks the database row.
  • Only one withdrawal of $100 succeeds.
  • The second request is rejected with "Insufficient Funds."
  • Final account balance is $0 (not -$100).

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
The security and backend data integrity testing phase for the Core Banking Application (Release 2.1) has concluded. However, two security vulnerabilities were identified and require immediate hotfixes before UAT sign-off.

Session Management ❌ Failed Concurrent login rules not enforcing properly. RBAC (Role-Based Access) ✅ Passed API endpoints correctly check JWT scopes.

docs.text:

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text: This Test Strategy outlines the quality assurance approach for the "SecureBank Core Ledger System," a highly sensitive financial application handling user transactions, account management, and inter-bank transfers.

docs.title: 2. Core Quality Objectives
docs.text: Due to the financial nature of the application, the testing strategy prioritizes: 1. Zero Data Loss: 100% adherence to ACID properties in the database. 2. Absolute Security: Compliance with OWASP Top 10 and PCI-DSS standards. 3. High Availability: System must support 10,000 concurrent transactions with 99.99% uptime.

docs.title: A. Functional Testing
docs.text:
• Focus: Account creation, deposit, withdrawal, fund transfers, interest calculation.
  • Approach: 100% test coverage using Data-Driven Testing (DDT) to verify complex interest calculation formulas across multiple account tiers.

docs.title: B. Security Testing (P0 Priority)
docs.text:
• Focus: Penetration testing, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), Session hijacking prevention, SQL Injection, XSS.
  • Approach: Automated daily SAST (Static Application Security Testing) pipeline scans. Manual external penetration testing every quarter.

docs.title: C. Database and Integrity Testing
docs.text:
• Focus: Transaction rollbacks, race conditions, schema validation.
  • Approach: Extensive backend testing using automated SQL validation scripts.

docs.title: D. Performance Testing
docs.text:
• Focus: Peak hour load (e.g., end-of-month salary deposits).
  • Approach: Automated JMeter scripts integrated into Jenkins, running soak tests over 48-hour periods.

docs.title: 4. Test Environment Management
docs.text:
• Security Constraint: Production data (PII and financial records) is strictly prohibited in lower environments.
  • Solution: A dedicated Data Masking and Synthetic Data Generation tool will be used to populate the QA and Staging databases with realistic but fake user profiles.

docs.title: 5. Defect SLAs
docs.text: Severity Resolution Target Critical (S1 - e.g., Fund transfer failure) 2 Hours Major (S2 - e.g., Statement generation fails) 24 Hours Minor (S3 - e.g., UI misalignment) Next Sprint

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text: This Test Plan defines the approach for validating the "MedConnect FHIR API," a backend integration portal used by hospitals to securely fetch and update Electronic Health Records (EHR).

docs.title: 2. Testing Scope
docs.text:
• In Scope: All RESTful endpoints related to /patients, /observations (lab results), and /medications.
  • Out of Scope: The front-end React application used by doctors (handled by a separate UI automation team).

docs.title: 3. Core Quality Requirements
docs.text: Because this application handles sensitive Protected Health Information (PHI), the priorities are: 1. HIPAA Compliance: Data must be encrypted in transit (TLS 1.3) and at rest. 2. Schema Validation: Responses must strictly adhere to the HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) JSON standard. 3. Authorization: A hospital administrator from Clinic A must be mathematically blocked from querying patient data from Clinic B.

docs.title: A. Endpoint Functional Testing
docs.text:
• Verify all CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) against the patient database.
  • Assert HTTP Status Codes (200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404).

docs.title: B. Security & Authentication Testing (OAuth 2.0)
docs.text:
• Verify Bearer tokens expire exactly after 15 minutes.
  • Verify attempting to use an expired token returns 401 Unauthorized.
  • Verify Cross-Tenant Data Access restrictions (403 Forbidden).

docs.title: C. JSON Schema Validation
docs.text: • Verify the API response payload strictly matches the complex FHIR schema (e.g., ensuring patient.id is a UUID, patient.birthDate is ISO-8601 formatted).

docs.title: 5. Tools & Frameworks
docs.text:
• Manual Exploration: Postman (Collections and Environments).
  • Automated Regression: Python, Pytest, and the requests library.
  • CI/CD: GitHub Actions (Running tests on every Pull Request).

docs.title: 6. Deliverables
docs.text:
1. Complete Postman Collection export (with environment variables).
  2. Automated Pytest repository.
  3. Final API Execution Report.

import pytest

def test_get_patient_returns_200(valid_token):

docs.title: [BUG-API-01] Revoked JWT Tokens can still be used to fetch data (CRITICAL)
docs.text:
• Status: Open (P0)
  • Description: When calling POST /auth/revoke, the server returns 200 OK. However, if the client uses that exact same token in a subsequent GET /patients request, the server accepts it and returns patient data.
  • Impact: If a doctor logs out, a malicious actor who intercepted their token can continue querying medical records until the token's hard expiry time (15 minutes).
  • RCA: The backend is only verifying the mathematical signature of the JWT, but it is not checking the Redis blacklist cache to see if the token was manually revoked.

docs.title: 1.1 The Fundamentals of Agile Software Development
Agile Manifesto Values
docs.text:
The foundation of all Agile methodologies lies in the four core values of the Agile Manifesto: 1. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools. 2. Working software over comprehensive documentation. 3. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation. 4. Responding to change over following a plan.

(Note: While there is value in the items on the right, Agile values the items on the left more.)

docs.title: Whole Team Approach
docs.text: In Agile, quality is everybody's responsibility. The "whole team" (Developers, Testers, Product Owner, Scrum Master) works together to deliver a quality product. - Breaks down the silos between development and testing. - Enhances collaboration and communication. - Testers are involved early in the process (Shift-Left).

docs.title: Early and Frequent Feedback
docs.text: Agile relies on short iterations (sprints) to deliver working software frequently. This allows the team to: - Get feedback from stakeholders early. - Adjust requirements based on actual user needs. - Identify and fix defects quickly, reducing the cost of quality.

docs.title: Extreme Programming (XP)
docs.text: A software development methodology intended to improve software quality and responsiveness to changing customer requirements. - Core Practices: Pair programming, Test-Driven Development (TDD), Continuous Integration (CI), small releases, simple design.

docs.title: Scrum
docs.text: A lightweight framework that helps people, teams, and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. - Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers (includes Testers). - Events: Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective. - Artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment.

docs.title: Kanban
docs.text: A method to manage and improve work across human systems by balancing demands with available capacity. - Key Practices: Visualize the workflow (Kanban board), limit Work in Progress (WIP), manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops.

docs.title: Sample Exam Questions — Chapter 1
docs.text:
Q1. Which of the following is a core value of the Agile Manifesto? - A) Comprehensive documentation over working software. - B) Following a plan over responding to change. - C) Customer collaboration over contract negotiation. ✅ - D) Processes and tools over individuals and interactions.

Q2. What is the primary benefit of the "Whole Team" approach in Agile? - A) It allows developers to avoid testing entirely. - B) It ensures that only the Product Owner is responsible for quality. - C) It promotes collaboration and makes quality everyone's responsibility. ✅ - D) It eliminates the need for independent testing.

docs.title: ISTQB Agile Tester Extension — Chapter 2: Agile Testing Methods
docs.text: Study notes for ISTQB Agile Tester Extension exam preparation.

docs.title: 2.1 Agile Testing Principles, Practices, and Processes
Continuous Testing
docs.text: Testing is not a phase at the end of the sprint; it is an ongoing activity that happens concurrently with development. - Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Delivery (CD) pipelines heavily rely on automated tests to provide immediate feedback.

docs.title: Test-Driven Development (TDD)
docs.text: Writing automated unit tests before writing the production code. - Follows the Red-Green-Refactor cycle. - Primarily a developer practice, but testers help define the test cases.

docs.title: Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD)
docs.text: Writing acceptance tests before development begins, collaboratively defined by the whole team (Three Amigos: PO, Dev, Tester). - Helps clarify requirements and ensure everyone has the same understanding of "Done."

docs.title: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)
docs.text: A variant of TDD that focuses on the behavior of the system from the user's perspective, using natural language formats (Given/When/Then). - Facilitates communication between business stakeholders and technical team members.

docs.title: 2.2 Assessing Quality Risks and Estimating Test Effort
Quality Risk Analysis in Agile
docs.text: Risk analysis happens frequently, often during sprint planning or release planning. - The team identifies risks to product quality and prioritizes testing based on those risks. - Helps decide what to test manually, what to automate, and what not to test.

docs.title: Estimating Test Effort in Agile
docs.text: Agile teams estimate the effort for the entire user story, which includes development, testing, and other tasks required to meet the Definition of Done (DoD). - Techniques: Planning Poker, T-shirt sizing. - Estimation is a collaborative team effort.

docs.title: Exploratory Testing
docs.text: Unscripted, experience-based testing where test design, execution, and learning happen concurrently. - Highly valuable in Agile because it finds defects that scripted tests miss and adapts quickly to changes. - Often guided by a Test Charter and managed in Timeboxes (Sessions).

docs.title: Session-Based Testing
docs.text: A structured approach to exploratory testing. - Testers document their findings, bugs, and ideas in a session sheet during a fixed, uninterrupted timebox.

docs.title: Sample Exam Questions — Chapter 2
docs.text:
Q1. Which development approach involves writing tests from the user's perspective using natural language (e.g., Given/When/Then)? - A) Test-Driven Development (TDD) - B) Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) ✅ - C) Keyword-Driven Testing - D) Exploratory Testing

Q2. How is test estimation typically handled in an Agile team using Planning Poker? - A) The Test Manager estimates all testing tasks separately. - B) Testing effort is estimated collaboratively by the whole team as part of the overall user story estimation. ✅ - C) Estimation is not done in Agile; the team just tests until the timebox ends. - D) Only the developers estimate the effort, and testers adapt to it.

docs.title: ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 1: Fundamentals of Testing
docs.text: Study notes for ISTQB CTFL (Certified Tester Foundation Level) exam preparation.

docs.title: 1.1 Why Is Testing Necessary?
docs.text: Key Points to Remember: - Software with defects can cause financial loss, time waste, business reputation damage, and physical injury - Testing gives stakeholders confidence in software quality - Testing is a means of quality control - Testing helps meet contractual or legal requirements

docs.title: 1.2 What Is Testing?
docs.text:
Testing includes both dynamic activities (executing code) and static activities (reviews, inspections).

Testing objectives: 1. Evaluate work products (requirements, user stories, design, code) 2. Trigger failures and find defects 3. Ensure required coverage 4. Reduce risk of inadequate quality 5. Verify requirements fulfilled 6. Verify compliance with regulations 7. Provide information for decision-making

Remember: Testing objectives vary by context (development phase, test level, SDLC model)

docs.title: 1.3 Testing and Debugging
docs.text: Testing Debugging Shows failures caused by defects Finds, analyzes, and fixes defects Done by testers Done by developers Triggers failures Fixes root cause

docs.title: 1.4 The Seven Testing Principles
docs.text: # Principle Key Phrase 1 Testing shows presence of defects Not absence 2 Exhaustive testing impossible Use risk + priorities 3 Early testing saves time and money Shift left 4 Defects cluster 80/20 rule 5 Beware of pesticide paradox Update test cases 6 Testing is context-dependent No one-size-fits-all 7 Absence of errors fallacy Usability matters too

docs.title: 1.5 Test Process
docs.text: The fundamental test process has these activities (not necessarily sequential):

docs.title: Test Planning
docs.text:
• Defining scope, approach, resources, schedule
  • Identifying test items, features to test
  • Estimating effort and costs
  • Defining entry and exit criteria

docs.title: Test Monitoring and Control
docs.text:
• Ongoing comparison of actual vs planned progress
  • Taking corrective actions when necessary
  • Test metrics reporting

docs.title: Test Analysis
docs.text:
• "What to test?"
  • Analyzing test basis (requirements, design, code)
  • Identifying testable features and conditions

docs.title: Test Design
docs.text:
• "How to test?"
  • Designing test cases and test data
  • Identifying required infrastructure and tools

docs.title: Test Implementation
docs.text:
• "Do we have everything to run tests?"
  • Organizing test cases into test suites
  • Creating test scripts, preparing test data

docs.title: Test Execution
docs.text:
• Running tests in planned order
  • Recording results, comparing with expected
  • Logging defects

docs.title: Test Completion
docs.text:
• Closing defect reports, archiving artifacts
  • Creating test summary report
  • Lessons learned

docs.title: 1.6 Psychology of Testing
docs.text:
Why is it psychologically difficult? - Finding someone's bugs can feel confrontational - Authors are emotionally attached to their code - QA engineer must be diplomatic, constructive, and objective

Key mindset: - Test to find defects (not prove software works) - Report defects factually, without blame - Constructive communication with developers

docs.title: Sample Exam Questions — Chapter 1
docs.text:
Q1. Which of the following is NOT a valid objective of testing? - A) Find defects - B) Build confidence in software quality - C) Prove software is bug-free ✅ (CORRECT — testing cannot prove this) - D) Provide information for decision-making

Q2. Which principle states that fixing all defects doesn't necessarily mean the software will satisfy users? - A) Defect clustering - B) Pesticide paradox - C) Absence-of-errors fallacy ✅ - D) Context-dependent testing

Q3. What is the difference between a defect and a failure? - A defect is a flaw in the code; a failure is the observable wrong behavior when the defect is executed.

Q4. Testing that starts early in SDLC is referred to as: - Shift-left testing

ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 1 Complete Next: Chapter 2: Testing Throughout SDLC

docs.title: ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 2: Testing Throughout the SDLC
docs.text: Study notes for ISTQB CTFL (Certified Tester Foundation Level) exam preparation.

docs.title: 2.1 Software Development Lifecycle Models
docs.text: Testing must adapt to the software development lifecycle (SDLC) model being used.

docs.title: Sequential Development Models
docs.text:
• Waterfall: Phases occur sequentially (Requirements $\to$ Design $\to$ Code $\to$ Test $\to$ Deploy). Testing happens at the very end.
  • V-Model: Integrates testing throughout the SDLC. For every development phase, there is a corresponding testing phase (e.g., Requirements Analysis $\leftrightarrow$ Acceptance Testing, System Design $\leftrightarrow$ System Testing).

docs.title: Iterative and Incremental Development Models
docs.text:
• Iterative: Groups of features are specified, designed, built, and tested together in a series of cycles (e.g., Agile, Scrum, Kanban).
  • Incremental: Establishing requirements, designing, building, and testing a system in pieces.

docs.title: 2.2 Test Levels
docs.text: Test levels represent groups of test activities that are organized and managed together.

docs.title: 1. Component Testing (Unit Testing)
docs.text:
• Focus: Modules, programs, objects, classes.
  • Performed By: Developers.
  • Basis: Detailed design, code, data model.

docs.title: 2. Integration Testing
docs.text:
• Focus: Interactions between components or systems.
  • Types: Component Integration (interactions between units) and System Integration (interactions between different systems/microservices).
  • Performed By: Developers (Component) or Testers (System).

docs.title: 3. System Testing
docs.text:
• Focus: The behavior of the whole system/product.
  • Performed By: Independent testing team.
  • Basis: System and software requirement specifications, use cases.
  • Environment: Should resemble production as closely as possible.

docs.title: 4. Acceptance Testing
docs.text:
• Focus: Validation that the system meets user needs and is ready for deployment.
  • Performed By: Customers, end-users, or business stakeholders.
  • Types:
  • User Acceptance Testing (UAT)
  • Operational Acceptance Testing (OAT)
  • Contractual/Regulatory Acceptance Testing
  • Alpha & Beta Testing

docs.title: 2.3 Test Types
docs.text:
Test types are a group of test activities aimed at testing specific characteristics of a software system.

  1. Functional Testing: Evaluating functions the system should perform ("What" the system does). Evaluated via Black-box techniques.
  2. Non-functional Testing: Evaluating attributes of the system ("How well" the system behaves - e.g., usability, performance, security).
  3. White-box Testing: Testing based on an analysis of the internal structure of the component or system.
  4. Change-related Testing:
  5. Confirmation Testing (Re-testing): Executing tests that previously failed to verify a defect fix.
  6. Regression Testing: Executing tests to ensure that changes (fixes or enhancements) haven't broken existing functionality.

docs.title: 2.4 Maintenance Testing
docs.text: Done on an existing operational system, triggered by modifications, migration, or retirement. - Impact Analysis: Done to evaluate the changes made for a maintenance release and identify the intended consequences as well as expected side effects. This helps decide how much regression testing is needed.

docs.title: Sample Exam Questions — Chapter 2
docs.text:
Q1. Which of the following is a characteristic of good testing applicable to any lifecycle model? - A) Testing starts only after coding is complete. - B) Testers should only be involved in execution. - C) For every development activity, there is a corresponding test activity. ✅ - D) Only developers should perform component and integration testing.

Q2. What is the main purpose of confirmation testing (re-testing)? - A) To ensure no new defects were introduced. - B) To verify that the original defect has been successfully fixed. ✅ - C) To test the integration of new modules. - D) To test the system's performance under load.

ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 2 Complete Next: Chapter 3: Static Testing

docs.title: ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 3: Static Testing
docs.text: Study notes for ISTQB CTFL (Certified Tester Foundation Level) exam preparation.

docs.title: 3.1 Static Testing Basics
docs.text: Static Testing relies on the manual examination of work products (reviews) or tool-driven evaluation of code/models (static analysis) without executing the code.

docs.title: What Can Be Examined?
docs.text: Almost any work product: - Requirements specifications - Epics, user stories, acceptance criteria - Architecture and design specifications - Code - Test plans, test cases, test scripts - User manuals

docs.title: Static vs. Dynamic Testing
docs.text:
• Static Testing: Finds the causes of failures (defects) directly. e.g., finding a variable that is not initialized.
  • Dynamic Testing: Finds the failures caused by defects. e.g., the program crashes when it runs.

Benefits of Static Testing: - Detects defects early (Shift-Left). - Cheaper to fix defects found before execution. - Finds defects that dynamic testing easily misses (e.g., unreachable code, design flaws).

docs.title: 3.2 Review Process
docs.text: Reviews vary from informal to highly formal.

docs.title: Roles in a Formal Review
docs.text:
1. Author: Creates the work product, fixes defects found.
  2. Management: Responsible for planning, assigning resources, and deciding if reviews are needed.
  3. Facilitator (Moderator): Ensures effective running of meetings, manages time, mediates disputes.
  4. Review Leader: Takes overall responsibility for the review.
  5. Reviewers (Inspectors): Subject matter experts who identify and describe anomalies (defects).
  6. Scribe (Recorder): Documents anomalies, decisions, and new defects found during the meeting.

docs.title: 3.3 Types of Reviews
docs.text: Review Type Characteristics Formality Informal Review No formal process. e.g., Buddy check, pairing. Widely used in Agile. Low Walkthrough Led by the Author. Scenario execution, dry runs. Used for learning and gaining consensus. Low to Medium Technical Review Documented, defined defect-detection process. Led by a trained moderator or tech expert. Peer review. Medium to High Inspection Most formal. Led by a trained Moderator (not the author). Uses checklists, metrics are collected, defined entry/exit criteria. High

docs.title: 3.4 Review Techniques
docs.text: Techniques reviewers use to uncover defects during the individual review phase: 1. Ad hoc: Reviewers are given little/no guidance. Highly dependent on reviewer skills. 2. Checklist-based: Reviewers use a list of questions or rules to guide the review. 3. Scenarios and dry runs: Reviewers are provided structured guidelines to process the work product like a user would. 4. Perspective-based: Reviewers evaluate the product from different viewpoints (e.g., end-user, system administrator, tester). 5. Role-based: Reviewers act as specific stakeholder roles (e.g., experienced user, manager).

docs.title: Sample Exam Questions — Chapter 3
docs.text:
Q1. Which of the following review types is usually led by the author? - A) Inspection - B) Technical Review - C) Walkthrough ✅ - D) Static Analysis

Q2. Which defect is easier to find in static testing than dynamic testing? - A) A memory leak under heavy load. - B) A deviation from coding standards. ✅ - C) A UI rendering issue on a specific browser. - D) An integration failure between two APIs.

ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 3 Complete Next: Chapter 4: Test Techniques

docs.title: ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 4: Test Techniques
docs.text: Study notes for ISTQB CTFL (Certified Tester Foundation Level) exam preparation.

docs.title: 4.1 Categories of Test Techniques
docs.text:
Test techniques help derive test conditions, test cases, and test data. They are divided into three categories:

  1. Black-box Techniques (Specification-based): Based on analyzing the test basis (requirements, specs, user stories). Treats software as a black box; no knowledge of internal code.
  2. White-box Techniques (Structure-based): Based on analyzing the internal structure (code, architecture).
  3. Experience-based Techniques: Based on the tester's knowledge, experience, and intuition.

docs.title: 1. Equivalence Partitioning (EP)
docs.text: Divides inputs into partitions where the system is expected to treat all values in that partition the same way. - Rule: Test one value from each valid and invalid partition.

docs.title: 2. Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)
docs.text: Tests the edges of Equivalence Partitions. Defects commonly cluster at boundaries. - Rule (2-value approach): Test the exact boundary and the value just outside it. (e.g., if valid is $1 \le x \le 10$, test $0, 1$ and $10, 11$). - Rule (3-value approach): Test before, at, and after the boundary (e.g., $0, 1, 2$ and $9, 10, 11$).

docs.title: 3. Decision Table Testing
docs.text: Used for testing complex business logic and combinations of conditions. - Conditions (inputs) and Actions (outputs) are mapped in a table. Each column represents a specific business rule.

docs.title: 4. State Transition Testing
docs.text: Used when the system can be in different states, and transitions from one state to another are triggered by events. - Derives test cases from a state transition diagram or table (State, Event, Action, Next State).

docs.title: 5. Use Case Testing
docs.text: Tests derived from Use Cases. Focuses on the interactions between actors (users/systems) and the system. Good for end-to-end integration testing.

docs.title: 1. Statement Testing and Coverage
docs.text: Ensures that executable statements in the code are executed at least once. - Formula: $\text{Statement Coverage} = \frac{\text{Number of executed statements}}{\text{Total number of statements}} \times 100\%$

docs.title: 2. Decision Testing and Coverage
docs.text: Ensures that decision outcomes (True and False branches of if statements) are executed. - Formula: $\text{Decision Coverage} = \frac{\text{Number of executed decision outcomes}}{\text{Total number of decision outcomes}} \times 100\%$ - Note: 100% decision coverage guarantees 100% statement coverage (but not vice-versa).

docs.title: 1. Error Guessing
docs.text: Anticipating where errors might occur based on the tester's past experience with similar applications. Often documented in a defect attack list.

docs.title: 2. Exploratory Testing
docs.text: Concurrent test design, test execution, test logging, and learning. Guided by a test charter. Excellent when specifications are poor or time is limited.

docs.title: 3. Checklist-based Testing
docs.text: Testers use a high-level list of items to be noted, checked, or remembered.

docs.title: Sample Exam Questions — Chapter 4
docs.text:
Q1. An input field takes a year of birth between 1900 and 2004. What are the boundary values using the 2-value BVA approach? - A) 1899, 1900, 2004, 2005 ✅ - B) 1900, 2004 - C) 1899, 1900, 1901, 2003, 2004, 2005 - D) 1899, 2005

Q2. Which technique is best for verifying different system behaviors based on previous history/status? - A) Equivalence Partitioning - B) Decision Table Testing - C) State Transition Testing ✅ - D) Use Case Testing

ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 4 Complete Next: Chapter 5: Test Management

docs.title: ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 5: Test Management
docs.text: Study notes for ISTQB CTFL (Certified Tester Foundation Level) exam preparation.

docs.title: Roles in Testing
docs.text:
1. Test Manager: Responsible for overall test planning, monitoring, control, and strategy. Reports on metrics.
  2. Tester: Responsible for reviewing requirements, setting up the test environment, writing test cases, executing tests, and logging defects.

docs.title: Independence of Testing
docs.text: Degrees of independence (from lowest to highest): 1. No independence: Developers test their own code. 2. Developers test each other's code. 3. Independent test team within the project. 4. Independent test team outside the project (e.g., separate QA department). 5. External test specialists (outsourced QA).

docs.title: 5.2 Test Planning and Estimation
docs.text:
Test Plan: Documents the approach, resources, and schedule of testing activities. - Test Strategy: General approach to testing (Organizational level). - Test Approach: Implementation of the strategy for a specific project.

Entry Criteria: Conditions that must be met before testing can start (e.g., environment is ready, code is deployed). Exit Criteria: Conditions that must be met to declare testing finished (e.g., 100% tests executed, 0 critical defects open).

docs.title: Test Estimation Techniques
docs.text:
1. Metrics-based technique: Estimating based on metrics of former, similar projects (e.g., Function Point Analysis).
  2. Expert-based technique: Estimating based on the experience of owners of the testing tasks (e.g., Planning Poker, Wideband Delphi).

docs.title: 5.3 Test Monitoring and Control
docs.text:
• Test Monitoring: Continuously gathering metrics to evaluate progress against the test plan. (e.g., % of test cases executed, defect density).
  • Test Control: Taking corrective actions when monitoring shows deviation from the plan. (e.g., re-prioritizing tests, adding resources).

docs.title: 5.4 Configuration Management
docs.text: Ensures the integrity of work products (code, test scripts, requirements) by tracking versions and managing updates. Ensures testers are testing the correct version of the software with the correct version of test scripts.

docs.title: 5.5 Risks and Testing
docs.text:
Risk involves the possibility of a negative event. $\text{Level of Risk} = \text{Probability} \times \text{Impact}$.

  1. Product Risk (Quality Risk): The risk that the software fails to satisfy user needs. (e.g., crash, security vulnerability, wrong calculation).
  2. Project Risk: The risk that the project management processes fail. (e.g., budget run out, key tester gets sick, test environment is offline).

Risk-Based Testing: Prioritizing testing effort based on product risks. High-risk areas are tested first and more rigorously.

docs.title: 5.6 Defect Management
docs.text:
A defect report must provide developers with the information needed to reproduce and fix the bug.

Common Defect Report Fields: - Identifier (ID) - Title and summary - Date, author - Test environment details - Steps to reproduce - Expected and Actual results - Severity (technical impact) and Priority (business urgency) - Status (Open, Fixed, Closed, etc.)

docs.title: Sample Exam Questions — Chapter 5
docs.text:
Q1. Which of the following is a Product Risk? - A) The test environment is not ready on time. - B) A third-party API integration returns incorrect data. ✅ - C) The QA Lead leaves the company. - D) The project budget is cut by 20%.

Q2. Who is typically responsible for setting up the test environment? - A) Test Manager - B) Project Manager - C) Tester ✅ - D) Product Owner

ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 5 Complete Next: Chapter 6: Tool Support for Testing

docs.title: ISTQB Foundation Level — Chapter 6: Tool Support for Testing
docs.text: Study notes for ISTQB CTFL (Certified Tester Foundation Level) exam preparation.

docs.title: 6.1 Test Tool Considerations
docs.text: Tools support testing activities to improve efficiency, reduce repetitive tasks, and automate validations.

docs.title: Purpose of Tools
docs.text:
• Improve efficiency of manual tasks.
  • Automate repetitive tasks (e.g., regression testing).
  • Perform activities that cannot be done manually (e.g., large scale performance testing).
  • Increase reliability of testing (consistent execution).

docs.title: 6.2 Classification of Test Tools
docs.text:
Tools are classified based on the testing activities they support.

  1. Tools for Management of Testing and Tests:
  2. Test Management Tools (TestRail, Zephyr)
  3. Requirements Management Tools (Jira, Confluence)
  4. Defect Management Tools (Jira, Bugzilla)

  5. Configuration Management Tools (Git, SVN)

  6. Tools for Static Testing:

  7. Review process support tools

  8. Static analysis tools (SonarQube) - usually used by developers.

  9. Tools for Test Design and Implementation:

  10. Test design tools (Model-based testing tools)
  11. Test data preparation tools (Faker)

  12. Test-driven development (TDD) tools

  13. Tools for Test Execution and Logging:

  14. Test Execution Tools (Selenium, Cypress, JUnit)
  15. Coverage Measurement Tools (JaCoCo)

  16. Test Harness / Unit Test Framework Tools

  17. Tools for Performance and Monitoring:

  18. Performance Testing Tools (JMeter, LoadRunner, k6)
  19. Dynamic Analysis Tools (Detect memory leaks)

docs.title: 6.3 Benefits and Risks of Test Automation
Potential Benefits
docs.text:
• Reduction in repetitive manual work.
  • Greater consistency and repeatability.
  • Objective assessment (removes human error).
  • Ease of access to information about tests or testing.

docs.title: Potential Risks
docs.text:
• Unrealistic expectations ("Automation will fix everything").
  • Underestimating the time, cost, and effort for initial introduction.
  • Underestimating the time and effort needed to maintain test scripts.
  • Over-reliance on the tool (ignoring exploratory testing).

docs.title: 6.4 Effective Tool Introduction
docs.text:
Introducing a tool into an organization should be done systematically.

Main Principles: 1. Assess organizational maturity and identify opportunities for tool use. 2. Evaluate tools against clear requirements and objective criteria. 3. Run a Proof of Concept (PoC) to verify the tool works with the actual application under test. 4. Evaluate the vendor (support, training, licensing). 5. Identify internal coaching and mentoring needs.

Pilot Project Objectives: - Learn more details about the tool. - Evaluate how the tool fits into existing processes. - Decide on standard ways of using, managing, and storing the tool's assets (e.g., naming conventions). - Assess whether the benefits will be achieved at a reasonable cost.

docs.title: Sample Exam Questions — Chapter 6
docs.text:
Q1. Which tool is most likely to be used by developers rather than testers? - A) Test management tool - B) Static analysis tool ✅ - C) Performance testing tool - D) Defect tracking tool

Q2. What is the primary purpose of executing a Pilot Project when introducing a new tool? - A) To train all testers in the organization immediately. - B) To learn how the tool fits into existing processes and define standards. ✅ - C) To roll out the tool to the entire company. - D) To automate all existing manual test cases.
